photos.k: How is a suspension bridge different from other bridges?

photos.t: The Cannon Mons Meg at Edinburgh
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Mons Meg is a huge medieval cannon at Edinburgh Castle that once fired stone balls. A guard stands beside it, so you can see how enormous it is.
photos.k: How tall is the guard compared with the cannon?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Hippolyte Bayard photographed a narrow street in Paris, with tall houses on one side and a quiet curve ahead. It shows the city before the wide boulevards were built.
photos.k: Find the chimney pots on the rooftops.
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 16 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.why: A Romanian historian and revolutionary leader sits for a portrait in Paris in 1846. He helped lead an uprising in Wallachia two years later.
photos.k: What do you think he is dreaming of?

photos.why: Thomas Carlyle was a Scottish writer and historian whose books were read all over the English-speaking world. This daguerreotype shows him as a serious man in a dark coat.
photos.k: What would you ask a historian?

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Hill and Adamson photographed Scots Guards soldiers at Edinburgh Castle in 1846. A group portrait with a camera was much faster than painting each soldier, so photography began to replace painted portraits.
photos.k: Why would a camera be quicker than a painter?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.t: St. Andrews Castle, from the Southeast
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: The two Scottish photographers visited this ruined castle in 1846. They liked old buildings because the soft paper negatives made them look moody and ancient.
photos.k: What mood does the ruined castle give you?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.cr: Gift of Michael Mattis and Judith Hochberg
photos.why: John Stewart photographed the new road through a rocky gorge in the Pyrenees. British tourists came here by carriage in the 1840s.
photos.k: How would you travel along this road?
photos.pr: salt print from a waxed paper negative

photos.why: Talbot photographed this street from a hotel window in Frankfurt in 1846. Looking out a window was an easy way to photograph with a heavy camera.
photos.k: What would you see from your window?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Calvert Richard Jones, who was a clergyman, photographed the harbor of Santa Lucia in Naples, Italy, in 1846. He used paper negatives, which gave the picture soft light.
photos.k: What might a harbor have looked like 180 years ago?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: Calvert Jones photographed a tall monument in Naples in 1846. His soft paper pictures were a bit like drawings made of light.
photos.k: What does an obelisk look like?
photos.pr: Salted paper print from a calotype negative

photos.cr: Major Acquisitions Centennial Endowment
photos.why: Frederick Douglass escaped from slavery as a young man and became one of the greatest speakers and writers in American history. He believed photographs showed Black Americans as dignified people, and he sat for more portraits than any other American of his century.
photos.k: He looks right at you. What do you think he wants you to feel?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Bayard photographed the oldest standing bridge in Paris, the Pont Neuf, with riverside houses and barges. The view looks much as it did centuries before, and today.
photos.k: Find the boats along the river.
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 14 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.t: La Fontaine du square de l'Archevêché; Derrière Notre-Dame
photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Hippolyte Bayard photographed a fountain behind Notre-Dame in Paris in 1847. His views of the city are some of the oldest we have, showing it before big rebuilding changed the streets.
photos.k: What would you see if you stood here today?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 19 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Louis-Rémy Robert, who was trained as a painter on porcelain, photographed the doorway of the Sèvres porcelain factory. Photographs of buildings like this are among the first ever.
photos.k: What do you think was made inside?
photos.pr: salted paper print, waxed, from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Hippolyte Bayard photographed a trellis, a wooden frame that holds up climbing plants, in 1847. It is a very early picture of a garden structure with light and shadow.
photos.k: What would grow on a trellis?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 5 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-1850

photos.why: Hermann Biow photographed the Brothers Grimm in 1847. Jacob and Wilhelm Grimm collected fairy tales like Cinderella, Snow White and Hansel and Gretel.
photos.k: Which Grimm fairy tale is your favorite?

photos.why: Peter von Cornelius was a famous German painter. Hermann Biow photographed him in Berlin in 1847.
photos.k: Why would a painter pose for a photographer?

photos.why: Stelzner photographed the Adolphsplatz in Hamburg in 1847. His pictures of the city are valuable because much of it was burned in the 1842 fire.
photos.k: Which buildings do you think survived the fire?

photos.why: Alexander von Humboldt was a famous German scientist and explorer who traveled to South America. Hermann Biow photographed him in Berlin in 1847.
photos.k: What would you like to ask an explorer?

photos.why: Hill and Adamson photographed Elizabeth Rigby, who later became Lady Eastlake, an art writer. Their calotype portraits were praised for their soft light and strong mood.
photos.k: What mood does the soft light give?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mr. and Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: In February 1848, Parisians built barricades in the streets and overthrew their king. Bayard photographed the Rue Royale just after the fighting, with paving stones torn up and a few barricades left.
photos.k: What do you think happened here a few days before?
photos.pr: Gelatin silver print, No. 12 from the portfolio "Bayard: XXV Calotypes, 1842-185

photos.cr: Gift of the Blum-Kovler Foundation
photos.why: Platt Babbitt was the official photographer at Niagara Falls and sold daguerreotypes to tourists. It is one of the earliest photographs of the great waterfall.
photos.k: What sounds do you imagine you would hear here?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: Talbot photographed this Spanish palace, with its decorated arches, in 1848. Pictures of far-off landmarks made travelers at home feel as if they had been there.
photos.k: Look at the arches. What patterns can you spot?

photos.t: Fountain of Notre-Dame at Saint-Brieuc, Brittany
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Louis-Rémy Robert photographed this fountain in Brittany in the late 1840s. Photographers like him hoped their pictures could be turned into prints that anyone could buy.
photos.k: Where does the water come from in this picture?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Henri Le Secq photographed a farm built into the soft rock of the French countryside. He had been a painter, and he used the same eye for shape and shadow.
photos.k: Where does the building stop and the rock begin?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Gift of Charles Isaacs and Carol Nigro
photos.why: Louis-Rémy Robert photographed himself on waxed paper negatives he made in the early 1850s. He later worked at the famous Sèvres factory.
photos.k: What do you see in his expression?

photos.t: St. Anthony Falls from Across the River
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: An unknown photographer made an instantaneous daguerreotype of the falls on the Mississippi River in Minnesota in 1848. The falling water looks sharp for a moment, which was a big achievement for the time.
photos.k: Is the water blurry or sharp? Why is that surprising?

photos.why: Dolley Madison was the wife of the fourth U.S. president, James Madison, and a famous Washington hostess. Mathew Brady photographed her in the late 1840s when she was an old woman.
photos.k: What do you think she was like?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Robert Browning, the poet, made a picture of his young son, Pen. His wife was the poet Elizabeth Barrett Browning, and their son was a favorite subject.
photos.k: What would you say to a poet's son?

photos.cr: Gift of Mr. and Mrs. Frank Kolodny
photos.why: Talbot photographed a fern branch in 1848. Plants were a favorite subject for him because he began his experiments with leaves and flowers.
photos.k: How many parts does a fern leaf have?
photos.pr: Photoglyphic engraving made without a gauze or resin ground screen

photos.why: Thomas Pratt was a lawyer and politician from Maryland who served as governor and U.S. senator. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1840s or 1850s.
photos.k: What would you ask a governor?

photos.t: Path in the Forest of Fontainebleau
photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed sun and shade on a forest path near Paris, where painters also went to paint. His soft paper prints show light the way an artist would.
photos.k: Where does the path lead?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.why: Edgar Allan Poe, who wrote spooky poems and stories like The Raven, was photographed in 1849, the last year of his life. The picture is a copy of a daguerreotype.
photos.k: Poe wrote about ravens and mysteries. What story would you tell with a face like this?

photos.why: Le Gray photographed an old tree growing between rocks in Fontainebleau Forest. The picture has deep shadows and bright patches, almost like a painting.
photos.k: How would you describe the tree's shape?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Ernest de Caranza was a French engineer in Istanbul who took up photography. He photographed a fountain in a city that was then called Constantinople.
photos.k: Fountains were places to meet. Where do people meet in your town?
photos.pr: salted paper print from paper negative

photos.t: The Temple of Isis at Philae
photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
photos.why: Maxime Du Camp took this photograph on an island in the Nile in Egypt in 1849. The temple was built over 2,000 years ago, and he was one of the first photographers to show Egypt to the world.
photos.k: What do the columns and walls look like up close?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Maxime Du Camp photographed the pyramid of Khafre at Giza in 1849. His pictures of Egypt helped start the fashion for photographing faraway places.
photos.k: How big do you think the pyramid is?

photos.t: Karnak, Gateway of the Temple of Khonsu
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Du Camp photographed a huge gateway at Karnak in Egypt, one of the biggest temple complexes in the world. His pictures were published in an album that became famous.
photos.k: What do the figures carved on the gateway show?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Du Camp photographed a temple in Egypt in 1849, when many ancient buildings were still half buried. The picture was printed in an album of his Egypt trip.
photos.k: Why were so many temples half buried?

photos.why: John C. Calhoun was a powerful senator from South Carolina who strongly defended slavery. Mathew Brady photographed him in March 1849, a year before he died.
photos.k: What do you notice about his face and eyes?

photos.why: This daguerreotype of Edgar Allan Poe was made in June 1849, a few months before he died. It is known as the Annie daguerreotype, because Poe gave it to his friend Annie Richmond.
photos.k: What do you think he is thinking about?

photos.t: The Pavillon de Flore and the Tuileries Gardens
photos.why: Marie-Charles-Isidore Choiselat photographed a wing of the Tuileries Palace and its gardens in Paris in 1849. The palace was burned down in 1871.
photos.k: Why would a view of a lost building be valuable?

photos.why: Cornelius Vanderbilt was a shipping and railroad tycoon who became one of the richest people in America. This portrait was made by the Brady studio around 1849.
photos.k: How do you think wealth showed in a portrait?

photos.why: Roger Taney was Chief Justice of the United States. Brady photographed him in 1849 as part of his collection of famous Americans.
photos.k: What does a chief justice's face say about his job?

photos.why: Martin Van Buren was the eighth president of the United States. This daguerreotype was taken around 1849 by Mathew Brady's studio, after he left the presidency.
photos.k: Which president would you like to photograph today?

photos.why: Frederick Langenheim and his brother William ran a studio in Philadelphia. They made some of the first photographs on glass slides, and Frederick was photographed around 1849.
photos.k: How are photographs on glass different from paper?

photos.why: Frederick Langenheim looks over some Talbotypes, the early paper photographs invented by Talbot. The Langenheims bought the American rights to Talbot's process in 1849.
photos.k: Why would Frederick buy a process?

photos.t: Zachary Taylor at the White House
photos.why: Mathew Brady took this daguerreotype of President Zachary Taylor at the White House in 1849. It is among the earliest photographs of a sitting president.
photos.k: How would you feel photographing the president?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Two people sit close together in this small daguerreotype, a picture on a mirror-polished silver plate. Each daguerreotype is one of a kind, and you have to tilt it to see the image. They were kept in little cases to protect the silver.
photos.k: They had to sit very still. How long can you hold a smile without moving?

photos.t: A Young Woman in a Daguerreotype
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: A young woman looks calmly at the camera in this daguerreotype from around 1850. The mirror-bright metal plate makes the picture seem to float.
photos.k: Imagine she is looking at you. What might she say?

photos.cr: Henry Foundation Fund
photos.why: On the left is a dried fern, on the right a blue cyanotype of a fern. John Herschel invented the cyanotype in 1842, and it is the process behind blueprints.
photos.k: How are the real fern and its blue print alike? How are they different?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Maxime Du Camp traveled up the Nile with the writer Gustave Flaubert and photographed what he found. This mosque with its slim minaret stands at the edge of old Cairo.
photos.k: Find the minaret. What does it look like?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Du Camp photographed the Sphinx straight on, with the pyramids behind. His pictures made Egypt look real to people who might never travel there.
photos.k: Imagine standing where the camera stood. What would you see around you?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: An ancient Egyptian temple on the Nile, half ruined and filled with sand. Du Camp's pictures helped Europeans fall in love with Egypt's past.
photos.k: How many columns can you count?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Four tall columns stand in the desert in Nubia, a region of the upper Nile. Du Camp carried his camera and glass plates by boat and camel to reach places like this.
photos.k: How would you carry delicate glass plates across a desert?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Du Camp photographed a gigantic statue of Pharaoh Ramses II at Abu Simbel and had a man stand by to show its scale. The statue is partly buried in sand, with a tiny figure at the right.
photos.k: Find the person. How big is the statue compared to him?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in memory of her mother Kathleen W. Harvey
photos.why: A group of street musicians stands in a Paris courtyard, each in worn clothes. Charles Nègre posed them to look natural, which was difficult when exposures took many seconds.
photos.k: What instruments do you think they played?
photos.pr: Photogravure, from the portfolio "Charles Negre: Treize Heliogravures, 1854–1857

photos.cr: Gift of Robert Jesmer
photos.why: Two almost identical pictures of the full moon sit side by side, made for a stereoscope. The first photographs of the Moon were made in the 1840s and 50s, and they showed people its craters for the first time.
photos.k: Can you spot dark patches on the Moon? Those are the lunar seas.

photos.why: Albert Southworth and Josiah Hawes ran the most famous daguerreotype studio in Boston. Their sitters look natural instead of stiff, and this woman in profile, with her hair swept neatly back, shows their quiet style.
photos.k: What can you tell about her from the way she holds her head?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean Levy and the Estate of Julien Levy
photos.why: Antoine Samuel Adam-Salomon trained as a sculptor before he took up photography. He lit faces like carved busts, with dramatic shadows that made his portraits famous.
photos.k: Which side of the face is lit? Which is in shadow?

photos.t: Portrait of a French Military Officer
photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Anstiss and Ronald Krueck
photos.why: A French military officer posed for this early portrait. Soldiers liked to have a picture to send home, and the stiff pose is partly because they had to hold still.
photos.k: What details of the uniform can you see?

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: This picture shows a gorge in the Pyrenees mountains, where British tourists came for their holidays. Early photographers carried heavy cameras to scenery like this, so that people at home could see it.
photos.k: What would it be like to carry a camera up here?
photos.pr: salted paper print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Gustave de Beaucorps photographed a woman in Algeria in about 1850. Photographs from this time often show the clothing and customs of people across the world, though they were chosen by the photographer.
photos.k: What details of clothing do you notice?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.t: Black Horseman in Front of a Doorway
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: A man on a black horse poses in front of a doorway. Pictures of people on horseback had long been popular with painters, and early photographers copied the idea.
photos.k: How does the horse stand? Is it calm or restless?
photos.pr: salt print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: A child stands on a chair holding flowers, with a mother beside. Daguerreotypes became cheap enough that ordinary families could have a portrait for the first time.
photos.k: What do you think the child is holding?

photos.cr: Jo Hershey Selden Fund
photos.why: A mother poses with two children in a portrait by Jean-Baptiste Frénet. He was a painter who switched to photography, and his skill with composition shows.
photos.k: How are the three of them arranged?
photos.pr: salted paper print from a collodion negative

photos.why: Francis Frith photographed people and places in the Punjab in northern India. Frith was one of the first big travel photographers, and his prints sold across Britain.
photos.k: What do the clothes tell you about these people?

photos.t: Samadhi of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Lahore
photos.why: This shrine in Lahore marks the resting place of Maharaja Ranjit Singh, a ruler of the Sikh Empire. Early photographs of buildings like this give a picture of how they looked long ago.
photos.k: What shapes do you see in the roof and walls?

photos.why: A domed tomb in the Punjab, photographed with a large camera and printed on albumen paper. Photographers carried glass plates on carts and camels to reach places like this.
photos.k: How many domes or arches can you count?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Du Camp traveled up the Nile and photographed the giant carved temple at Abu Simbel, which was buried in sand at that time. His pictures made people in France excited about ancient Egypt.
photos.k: What do you think it was like to find a temple half buried in sand?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative, Blanquart-Évrard process

photos.cr: L. E. Holden Fund
photos.why: A little girl named Alice Montgomery sat for a daguerreotype portrait around 1850. Pictures of children were cherished, because the family could keep a copy forever.
photos.k: What is she holding or wearing?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Two children pose with their toys in a daguerreotype made around 1850. Children had to sit very still for the exposure, so their toys helped keep them calm.
photos.k: What toys would you have taken to be photographed?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: A child holds a toy drum in a daguerreotype made around 1850. The unknown photographer worked hard with a heavy camera to capture a moving child.
photos.k: What sound would the drum make?

photos.t: Artist with His Palette and Brushes
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: An unknown photographer made a personal portrait of a painter holding his tools. The daguerreotype shows how artists and photographers learned from each other.
photos.k: What do his tools tell you about his job?

photos.t: The Music Teacher and His Wife
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: A music teacher and his wife posed for this daguerreotype, which shows how sitters could suggest how they wanted to look. The couple chose to show their love of music.
photos.k: What instrument do you see?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: John R. Johnston was an artist and musician who also made daguerreotypes. He made a portrait of his wife around 1850.
photos.k: Why might an artist take so many pictures of his family?
photos.pr: salted paper print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Gift of Charles Isaacs and Carol Nigro
photos.why: A young woman poses in pantalettes, the long ruffled underpants that girls wore under their dresses in the 1840s. Daguerreotypes like this one show us what people wore.
photos.k: What would be hard about wearing this every day?
photos.pr: daguerreotype, tinted and gilted highlights, half plate

photos.cr: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
photos.why: Louis Jules Duboscq-Soleil made this stereoscopic picture of a monkey on a branch. Stereoscopes showed two nearly identical pictures that seemed to pop out in 3D, and they were a big craze.
photos.k: How could two pictures make one 3D picture?

photos.cr: Hershey Family Art Purchase Fund
photos.why: It seemed a miracle that anyone could afford to have an accurate picture of themselves. This young woman sat for a daguerreotype around 1850, which cost much less than a painting.
photos.k: How would it feel to see yourself in a picture for the first time?

photos.t: The Great Temple of Isis at Philae
photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Purchase Fund
photos.why: Maxime Du Camp photographed this temple on an island in the Nile. It was later moved to a new island to save it from rising water, so his picture shows its original place.
photos.k: Why would a temple be moved?

photos.t: Workman in a Red Flannel Shirt
photos.cr: Gift of Nina Rosenblum and Lisa Rosenblum
photos.why: Daguerreotypes were mostly of wealthy people, but this one shows a laborer in a work shirt and suspenders. It is a rare picture of an ordinary worker around 1850.
photos.k: What do you think his job was?

photos.t: Adolescent Wearing Earrings and a Suit
photos.why: A 12-year-old poses for a daguerreotype in a suit and earrings. Early portraits show how people dressed up and how fashions have changed.
photos.k: What would you wear for a portrait?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Leigh B. Block
photos.why: Charles Clifford photographed the Gate of Forgiveness at Seville Cathedral in Spain in about 1850. He was a Welsh photographer who worked in Spain for Queen Isabella II.
photos.k: What patterns do you see on the arch?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. Leigh B. Block
photos.why: George Barker photographed Niagara Falls in 1850 and sold the pictures as stereographs to tourists. The water looks like cotton because it moved during the exposure.
photos.k: Why does the falling water look soft?

photos.why: John Bidwell was a California pioneer who later ran for president. This portrait was made from a daguerreotype Brady took of him around 1850.
photos.k: What do you think a pioneer looks like?

photos.why: James Fenimore Cooper wrote The Last of the Mohicans. This daguerreotype of the author was made by Mathew Brady around 1850.
photos.k: Have you read a book by this author?

photos.t: The Barley Mow Inn, Clifton Hampden
photos.why: Francis Frith photographed an old English pub with a thatched roof. Before he went to Egypt, Frith made a business of selling pictures of towns and villages.
photos.k: What would you like to eat at an old inn?

photos.why: Francis Frith photographed a street in Birmingham, England, where tall buildings and horse carts mix. It is a good example of how street photos show city life of the time.
photos.k: What would you notice about the traffic?

photos.why: This early photograph shows the Great Pyramid and the remains of a causeway leading to it. The pyramid was built about 4,500 years ago for Pharaoh Khufu.
photos.k: How do you think people moved the stones?

photos.why: Francis Frith photographed Conwy Castle in Wales, a big stone fortress built in the 1280s. His pictures of castles sold well to Victorian tourists.
photos.k: How many towers can you count?

photos.why: A tintype is a photograph made on a thin sheet of dark metal. It was cheap and quick to make, so ordinary people could afford portraits.
photos.k: What does her clothing tell you about her time?

photos.why: Baron Gros was a diplomat who photographed his own sitting room with a daguerreotype around 1850. Crowded with paintings and furniture, it shows how rich people decorated.
photos.k: How many paintings can you count?

photos.why: A tintype portrait of a man, printed on dark metal. These small pictures were sold at fairs and in towns for a small price.
photos.k: What do you think the man did for a living?

photos.why: Francis Frith's series included photographs of the cemetery in Lucknow, India. This tomb is for Brigadier-General James Neill, who died in the 1857 uprising.
photos.k: Why might people visit a cemetery from a faraway war?

photos.why: Two couples pose together for a tintype in the late 1800s. A tintype could be made in minutes, so friends could take one home the same day.
photos.k: Why would two couples want a picture together?

photos.why: Bertha Wehnert-Beckmann ran one of the first photography studios in Leipzig, Germany. This daguerreotype shows the glass-roofed room where she photographed her customers.
photos.k: Why would a photo studio need so much glass?

photos.why: Baron Jean-Baptiste Louis Gros photographed the entrance to the Acropolis in Athens in May or June 1850. It is one of the earliest photographs of the Parthenon site.
photos.k: Why would the Greeks care about the photograph?

photos.t: Madame Hahn and Her Seven Children
photos.why: J. Völlner photographed a mother with seven children in the mid-1800s. Family portraits like this were a point of pride, and a big family needed a big studio.
photos.k: How many children can you count?

photos.why: Nathaniel Parker Willis was a popular American poet and magazine editor. Mathew Brady's studio photographed him in the 1850s.
photos.k: What would a magazine editor like to read?

photos.why: Maxime Du Camp photographed a tall pillar in the temple area at Karnak, Egypt, around 1850. He was traveling with the writer Gustave Flaubert.
photos.k: Why would a writer travel with a photographer?

photos.why: Alois Löcherer photographed Franz Hanfstaengl, a famous artist and lithographer in Munich, around 1850. Hanfstaengl later became one of the best photographers in Germany.
photos.k: How can an artist become a photographer?

photos.t: Barefoot Boy with a Hat and a Drumstick
photos.why: A barefoot boy leans on a chair with a drumstick in a daguerreotype made around 1850. Children were photographed with toys to keep them still.
photos.k: What kind of toys can you hold while sitting still?

photos.why: Justus von Liebig was a German chemist who helped to create modern chemistry and invented fertilizer. Alois Löcherer photographed him around 1850.
photos.k: What would a chemist look like?

photos.why: Robert H. Vance made this ambrotype, a photograph on glass, of a boy from the Maidu people of California around 1850. Vance had a gallery in San Francisco in the Gold Rush years.
photos.k: What do you think the boy thinks about being photographed?

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed this old abbey church with its tall spire for the French government, which sent photographers to record historic buildings that needed repair. It was one of the first photo projects for protecting heritage.
photos.k: How tall is the spire compared with the church?

photos.why: In 1851 the French government sent five photographers on the Mission Héliographique to photograph historic buildings that needed protecting. Le Gray photographed the great church of Saint-Sernin and its tall octagonal tower.
photos.k: How many levels can you count in the tower?

photos.why: Le Gray photographed the old walls and towers of the medieval city of Carcassonne in France when they were crumbling. They were restored soon afterward, so pictures like this show the town before repairs.
photos.k: Count the round towers you can see.

photos.why: Thomas Easterly's daguerreotype shows a pond on the edge of St. Louis, Missouri, with horse-drawn wagons along the shore. The pond was drained and built over not long afterward.
photos.k: What would you see here today if you stood in the same place?

photos.t: Fourth and Olive Streets, St. Louis
photos.why: On a corner in St. Louis in 1851, awnings shade the shop windows and a horse-drawn wagon waits in the street. It is one of the earliest photographs of an American city street.
photos.k: What are the people and horses doing?

photos.cr: Gift of Arnold Gilbert
photos.why: This French photograph shows a statue from the Parthenon in Athens. It is one of the first pictures to record famous sculptures, so people could study them without traveling to see them.
photos.k: Does the sculpture look alive? How can you tell?

photos.t: Portico of the Château d'Anet, now at the École des Beaux-Arts, Paris
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Charles Marville photographed a stone doorway that was once part of a grand château and now stands in a Paris school. Marville is best known for recording old Paris streets before they were torn down.
photos.k: How can a piece of one building end up in another?
photos.pr: salted paper print, Blanquart-Évrard process, from waxed-paper negative

photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Trust
photos.why: Guillaume Duchenne used small electric shocks to make faces smile or frown, then photographed them. He wanted to find out how our faces make feelings. His pictures of expressions were one of the first science projects done with a camera.
photos.k: Make the same face. Which muscles move?
photos.pr: Albumen print from glass plate negative

photos.t: Studying the Muscles of Expression II
photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Trust
photos.why: Duchenne photographed how single muscles move the face when stimulated. His book showed readers the difference between a real smile and a fake one, and Charles Darwin later used his pictures.
photos.k: Do you know how to tell a real smile from a fake smile?
photos.pr: Albumen print from glass plate negative

photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Trust
photos.why: Guillaume Duchenne photographed an old man whose face muscles he made move with small electric shocks. These photographs were among the first used to study how faces show feelings.
photos.k: What does his face seem to say?
photos.pr: Albumen print from glass plate negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: In 1851 Gustave Le Gray and his friend Auguste Mestral traveled through southern France taking pictures for the government. This picture of an old bridge in Palalda shows the shapes of arches and shadows.
photos.k: How would you cross the bridge?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed-paper negative

photos.t: An Effect of the Sun, Normandy
photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Le Gray photographed sunlight breaking through clouds over the sea. He was one of the first to catch dramatic skies, and to do it he joined two negatives together.
photos.k: How does the light make the water look?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.t: The Large Speos at Abu Simbel
photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Félix Teynard was a civil engineer who photographed Egypt in 1851 and 1852. His photograph of the Great Temple at Abu Simbel shows the huge statues covered by sand.
photos.k: Why do you think the statues are partly buried?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.cr: Gift of Betty and Max Ratner in honor of Arielle Kozloff
photos.why: Teynard photographed the avenue of sphinxes at Karnak in Egypt, where statues with ram heads line the path. His pictures were known for their careful, calm look.
photos.k: What animal's head do the sphinxes have?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.t: The Royal Porcelain Factory at Sèvres
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Henri-Victor Regnault, a chemist, photographed the royal porcelain factory at Sèvres in France. He was a scientist who used photography to study how light and chemicals worked.
photos.k: Why would a chemist be interested in photography?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Southworth and Hawes, who ran a studio in Boston, made this large daguerreotype of a bride and her bridesmaids in 1851. Wedding pictures this early are rare.
photos.k: What do you notice about their dresses?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Frank Chauvassaignes made a mysterious landscape with a person resting by a stream. The sunlight and deep shadows make it look like a painting.
photos.k: What is the person doing by the stream?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Félix Teynard photographed temples cut straight into the rock in Egypt in 1851. He worked in heat and sand, and his pictures were published in a large album.
photos.k: How do you carve a whole temple out of a cliff?
photos.pr: salted paper print from a paper negative

photos.cr: Severance and Greta Millikin Trust
photos.why: Guillaume Duchenne photographed a man making a laughing face using electricity on his muscles. It was part of the first scientific study of how faces show feelings.
photos.k: Which muscles do you use to laugh?
photos.pr: Albumen print from glass plate negative

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed the east side of this castle, built across a river in France, in 1851. It is one of the oldest pictures of a famous castle.
photos.k: What is unusual about where this castle is built?

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed the west side of this French castle in 1851. Chenonceau is built right over the River Cher, which makes it look as if it floats.
photos.k: How is the castle different from most castles?

photos.why: Le Gray photographed the north side of Chenonceau in 1851. He and other photographers worked for the government to record old French buildings.
photos.k: Why would the government want these pictures?

photos.why: This close-up of Chenonceau by Le Gray shows the rooms of Queen Louise of Lorraine, a widow who lived there in the 1500s. The carved stone is crisp in the picture.
photos.k: What details do you notice up close?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in memory of her mother Kathleen W. Harvey
photos.why: Théophile Gautier was a French poet and novelist who believed that beauty was reason enough for art. Charles Nègre photographed him as a thoughtful man with a beard.
photos.k: What do you think he is looking at?
photos.pr: Photogravure, from the portfolio Charles Negre: Treize Heliogravures, 1854–1857

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Edward Byron Smith
photos.why: Benjamin Brecknell Turner took up photography as a hobby and carried a huge camera around the English countryside. His pictures show quiet scenes of trees, cottages and rivers.
photos.k: What is the weather like in this picture?

photos.cr: Gift of David C. and Sarajean Ruttenberg
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed the Louvre in Paris while it was being rebuilt. The French government hired him to record important buildings, and his sharp prints helped win photography respect.
photos.k: What would you want to see inside this building?

photos.cr: Edwin R. and Harriet Pelton Perkins Memorial Fund
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed the side of Notre-Dame cathedral with its tall flying buttresses, the stone arms that hold the walls up. He printed the picture from a large glass negative.
photos.k: Can you find the stone arms that prop up the walls?
photos.pr: salted paper print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Photography Discretionary Fund
photos.why: William Henry Pigou was a doctor and a part-time photographer working for the British in India. His pictures are some of the earliest of Indian temples.
photos.k: What details do you notice on the temple walls?

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed a man named Charles Delahaye in 1852. Before he became known for street scenes, Marville made portraits, and this is one of them.
photos.k: What does the sitter's expression tell you?

photos.t: Allegorical Sculpture of Industry, Pont du Carrousel
photos.why: Charles Marville photographed a statue of Industry on a Paris bridge. The sculptures were carved in stone, and Marville's picture shows their weight and shadow.
photos.k: What is the statue holding?

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: Anna Atkins made this picture of a fern by laying a leaf on light-sensitive paper and letting the sun print it blue. In 1843 she made the first book illustrated with photographs.
photos.k: Can you spot the tiny parts of the fern's leaf?

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Henri Le Secq photographed the northern side of Amiens Cathedral. Le Secq was a painter's son who photographed Gothic churches with extra care.
photos.k: How many levels of windows can you count?
photos.pr: salted paper print from calotype negative

photos.cr: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
photos.why: George Pugh was a senator from Ohio. Photographers displayed pictures of politicians in their windows as advertising.
photos.k: Why would a photographer put pictures of famous people in their window?
photos.pr: salted paper print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Louis-Rémy Robert photographed his daughter Henriette seated and looking at the camera. Parents were some of the best photographers of their children.
photos.k: What do you think she was doing when it was taken?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Gift of Susan Herzig and Paul Hertzmann, in memory of Robert P. Bergman
photos.why: Ingres was one of the most admired painters in France. He sat for this photograph in 1852, even though he thought painting was more serious than photography.
photos.k: Why would a painter let himself be photographed?
photos.pr: salted paper print from a paper negative

photos.t: Young Man in an Athletic Outfit
photos.cr: Gift of Charles Isaacs and Carol Nigro
photos.why: Oliver Willard photographed a young man in clothes for sports. People then played sports in clothes that looked like street clothes.
photos.k: How is his outfit different from what an athlete wears today?
photos.pr: salted paper print from wet collodion negative

photos.why: Charles Marville and Louis Désiré Blanquart-Évrard photographed a statue of Diana in the Louvre in 1852. The goddess stands with her deer, carved by famous sculptors.
photos.k: What is the goddess holding?

photos.t: Trees by the Chailly Road, Fontainebleau
photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed a forest road in Fontainebleau, where painters and photographers liked to work. The dark trees and bright road feel like a painting.
photos.k: Where does the road lead?

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed the art exhibition called the Salon of 1852 at the Palais-Royal in Paris. Paintings hung from floor to ceiling.
photos.k: How would you hang so many paintings?

photos.cr: Norman O. Stone and Ella A. Stone Memorial Fund
photos.why: John Beasley Greene was an American working in Egypt who photographed the Great Sphinx half buried in sand. At the time, the Sphinx was covered up to its shoulders, and you can see the pyramid beyond.
photos.k: How much of the Sphinx is buried in sand?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: According to legend, a nymph named Egeria met an ancient Roman king in this shady grotto and gave him advice. Robert MacPherson, a Scottish doctor living in Rome, photographed its mossy stones and trees.
photos.k: Why do you think people made up a story about a magical cave?

photos.cr: Gift of Leslie Stone Douglass
photos.why: This triumphal arch in the south of France was built about two thousand years ago. Édouard Baldus photographed it with huge paper negatives, so every carved detail shows.
photos.k: How many archways does it have?

photos.cr: Gift of Robert Hershkowitz and Charles Isaacs
photos.why: John Murray was a doctor who photographed the Taj Mahal and other great buildings in India. This tomb in Agra is sometimes called the baby Taj, and Murray's large prints sold across Britain.
photos.k: Look at the patterns on the walls. What shapes repeat?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Anstiss and Ronald Krueck in honor of Dr. Paul Urnes
photos.why: Auguste Mestral was one of five photographers hired by the French government in 1851 to record historic buildings. He photographed an angel sculpture in the Sainte-Chapelle in Paris.
photos.k: How would you pose like this angel?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Francis Frith traveled up the Nile in the 1850s and photographed temples half buried in sand. Kom Ombo is a temple to the crocodile god, and people in Britain were thrilled to see it.
photos.k: Why would people in Britain want to see this picture?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed the old market square in Mainz, Germany. The weekly market had been held there for centuries, and his picture records houses that were later lost.
photos.k: What buildings do you see around the square?

photos.cr: Mr. and Mrs. Richard W. Whitehill Art Purchase Endowment Fund
photos.why: Dr. John Murray photographed the Taj Mahal from the bank of the Yamuna River in the 1850s. It is a very early photograph of a world-famous building, taken by a doctor with a huge camera.
photos.k: What do you think it was like to carry such a camera in the heat?

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed this square in Mainz, Germany, named after Johannes Gutenberg, who invented the printing press. It is a nice fit that a photographer visited the town of printing.
photos.k: Why was printing an important invention?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Benjamin Brecknell Turner photographed tall pine trees in the English countryside. At a time of factories and trains, he chose quiet scenes of trees and old cottages.
photos.k: What do the tall trees feel like?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Frank Chauvassaignes photographed an artist, or maybe an assistant, smoking a pipe. The deep light and shadows make this portrait look like a painting from long ago.
photos.k: What do you think he is thinking about?
photos.pr: salt print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Auguste Mestral photographed a statue made for Notre-Dame in Paris around 1853. A sculptor had asked him to photograph his work.
photos.k: How might a photographer help a sculptor?
photos.pr: salted paper print from paper negative

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Nadar photographed Louis Figuier, a French scientist and writer of popular science books. Nadar's friends were often writers, artists and scientists.
photos.k: What would a science writer be doing?
photos.pr: Woodburytype, from the periodical “Galerie Contemporaine Littéraire, Artistique”

photos.cr: Dudley P. Allen Fund
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed the old Roman cemetery of Saint-Honorat near Arles, France, in 1853, on a trip to Provence. The long avenue of stone tombs gave a ruined, ancient mood.
photos.k: What makes a graveyard look ancient?
photos.pr: salt print from waxed paper negative

photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed a statue of the sculptor David d'Angers. David d'Angers was a famous French sculptor who made many monuments.
photos.k: Why might a sculptor like to be photographed?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: The Bisson brothers photographed the carvings over the doors of Chartres Cathedral, with Jesus seated in the middle and rows of small figures below. Their sharp pictures let people study the carvings without climbing up.
photos.k: How many figures can you find carved above the door?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Reproductions photographiques des plus beaux type

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Lucia Woods Lindley and Daniel A. Lindley, Jr.
photos.why: Huge carved columns rise at Medinet Habu in Egypt, a temple built for Pharaoh Ramses III more than three thousand years ago. John Beasley Greene was one of the first photographers to carry cameras up the Nile.
photos.k: How many people holding hands would it take to go around one column?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Helen Harvey Mills in memory of her mother Kathleen W. Harvey
photos.why: Auguste Salzmann photographed tombs carved in rock near Jerusalem to prove they were very old. His careful pictures were published in a large book and helped start the study of the city's ancient past.
photos.k: Find the doorways carved in the cliff.

photos.why: A smiling woman in a dark dress stands in a Boston studio. Southworth and Hawes asked their sitters to relax, and it shows.
photos.k: What do you think made her smile?

photos.why: William and Frederick Langenheim, brothers in Philadelphia, photographed the partial solar eclipse of May 1854 with a daguerreotype. The Sun shows as a thin crescent with the Moon covering the rest. Taking a picture of the Sun without damaging the camera was a challenge.
photos.k: Why do you think the Sun looks like a crescent? What is covering the other part?

photos.why: Thomas Easterly, a daguerreotypist in St. Louis, photographed the busy riverside streets of his city from rooftops. This view shows shops, signs and a growing town.
photos.k: Read the signs. What do you think each shop sold?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: The Bisson brothers, Louis-Auguste and Auguste-Rosalie, climbed with huge cameras to photograph French cathedrals. This doorway at Amiens is covered with saints and kings.
photos.k: How many carved figures can you count?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Reproductions photographiques des plus beaux type

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: The Bisson brothers photographed the south side of Chartres Cathedral. Their large photographs let people study carved details without climbing a scaffold.
photos.k: Can you find any carved saints in the doorway?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Reproductions photographiques des plus beaux type

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: This is the front of Chartres Cathedral in France, built more than 800 years ago. The Bisson brothers needed bright sunshine and a lot of patience to photograph it.
photos.k: The two towers are different. Can you spot how?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Reproductions photographiques des plus beaux type

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: The Bisson brothers photographed an ancient Roman arch built in the year 203. Their pictures showed travelers the ruins of Rome in sharp detail.
photos.k: What did this arch celebrate? Look at the carved figures.
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Reproductions photographiques des plus beaux type

photos.cr: Gift of David C. and Sarajean Ruttenberg
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed old water mills in the Auvergne region of France. His pictures mix people's work with the land, and the water looks silky because of the long exposure.
photos.k: Why does the water look smooth like silk?

photos.t: Sir Hy. Fk. Ponsonby (1825-1892) General; Thomas Hook Pearson (1806-1892) General; Fredric
photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed British officers in the Crimean War in 1854 and 1855. He was one of the first war photographers and had to haul a wagon-sized darkroom.
photos.k: Why would a photographer need a wagon for a camera?

photos.why: Marville photographed the doorway of Reims Cathedral in France. Kings of France were crowned there for centuries, and the stone carvings were so detailed that photographers wanted to record them.
photos.k: How many carved figures can you find?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Auguste Salzmann photographed the Tomb of the Virgin in Jerusalem in 1854. The French government sent him to take pictures of old buildings in the Holy Land.
photos.k: Why would a government send a photographer?
photos.pr: salted paper print, Blanquart-Évrard process, from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Julien Vallou de Villeneuve photographed Leroux, an actor from the Comédie-Française, in a role from Molière's play The Misanthrope. The actors posed for photographs like this to promote their shows.
photos.k: How would an actor pose to look like a character?
photos.pr: albumen print from wax paper negative

photos.t: Plaster Cast from the Depaulis Collection
photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Henri Le Secq photographed a plaster copy of a sculpture. Photographing plaster casts was good practice and also helped art students who could not travel.
photos.k: Why would art students want pictures of sculptures?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Mr. and Mrs. Richard W. Whitehill Art Purchase Endowment Fund
photos.why: An amateur photographer, known only as W.H.G., made this large and richly toned print of a house in Pau, France. Pau was a popular winter resort for British visitors.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a house like this?
photos.pr: salted paper print from a paper negative

photos.why: Nadar was a French photographer, balloonist and caricaturist who photographed the famous people of Paris. He made self-portraits with a wild mane of red hair and a bold look.
photos.k: What does his face show about his personality?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by William Mares
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed a rocky valley in France where a new railroad was going to run. He was hired to photograph railways and monuments, and he made them look grand.
photos.k: Where could a train run through this valley?

photos.t: The Valley of the Shadow of Death
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton named this road in Crimea after a Bible verse. Soldiers were fighting nearby, and cannonballs lay all over the ground. Fenton made two versions, one with cannonballs on the road and one without, and historians still argue which came first.
photos.k: The road is bare in this version. Where do you think the cannonballs went?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Graves of British officers who died in the Crimean War are marked with white stones on a bare hillside. Fenton's photographs were shown in London so the public could see what war was like.
photos.k: How does an empty hillside make you feel?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Lord Raglan, the British general, sits with other commanders outside a farmhouse, planning their next moves. Fenton was one of the first photographers to travel to a war zone, with a horse-drawn darkroom wagon.
photos.k: Who do you think is giving the orders?

photos.t: A Quiet Day in the Mortar Battery
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton's cameras were too slow to photograph fighting, so he photographed calm moments, like soldiers resting beside their heavy mortars. These pictures made the war look more peaceful than it really was.
photos.k: Which parts of a war can a camera not show?
photos.pr: Salted paper print,  from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Soldiers gather in thick coats beside a hut in the Crimean winter. Fenton's pictures showed families at home that their sons were surviving cold and mud.
photos.k: What would you wear in a cold camp like this?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 40 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.cr: Photography Associates Fund
photos.why: Adolphe Braun photographed the snowy Alps and sold his prints to travelers as souvenirs. He ran one of the largest photography businesses in France.
photos.k: Which peak do you think is the highest?

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: A paddle steamer glides on a Swiss lake with mountains behind. Braun's careful pictures made travel look elegant.
photos.k: Where do you think the steamer is heading?

photos.cr: Through prior purchase with Edward E. Ayer Endowment in memory of Charles L. Hutchinson
photos.why: Linnaeus Tripe joined a British mission to Burma in 1855 and photographed the temples of Pagan (Bagan), where thousands of temples rise from the plains. He printed large pictures on paper that show every carving.
photos.k: How many pointed shapes can you count on this temple?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Burma Views" (1857)

photos.t: The Tomb of the Christian Woman, Algeria
photos.cr: Gift of the Lunn Gallery
photos.why: A great round tomb with a stepped roof stands near Algiers. It was built long ago for a king and queen of Mauretania, but local people told stories of a Christian woman buried within.
photos.k: What shape does the tomb remind you of?

photos.why: A dog sits upright in a chair in a photo studio, as if it were a member of the family. Pets were hard to photograph, but families wanted to remember them too.
photos.k: What do you think the dog was waiting for?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed generals and soldiers in Crimea in 1855. He did not show fighting because cameras were too slow, but his portraits put faces on a distant war.
photos.k: What do you notice about the general's uniform?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed a cavalry camp during the Crimean War. The horses and tents tell us how soldiers lived, even though cameras of the time could not capture battles.
photos.k: What would life in this camp be like?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton's camp pictures show lines of tents and horses on the hills of Crimea. The war lasted from 1853 to 1856, and his photographs were seen by people at home in Britain.
photos.k: Can you find the horses?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed this British general in the Crimea in 1855. Windham was known for leading an attack during the war.
photos.k: What do you see in the general's face?

photos.cr: Gift of Robert A. Taub
photos.why: Baldus photographed the Madeleine in Paris, a church that looks like a Greek temple. He chose a calm view so that the columns lined up like a row of soldiers.
photos.k: How many columns do you see?

photos.cr: Smart Family Acquisition Fund
photos.why: Linnaeus Tripe produced some of the earliest photographs of British India and Burma. This monastery building, called a kyaung, was photographed on a trip to document the region.
photos.k: What material do you think the building is made of?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Views of Burma" (1856)

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Lucia Woods Lindley and Daniel A. Lindley, Jr.
photos.why: Charles Clifford photographed the famous courtyard of the Alhambra in Granada, Spain. The slender columns and the fountain of lions made it one of Europe's most photographed places.
photos.k: How many columns can you count?

photos.t: Kadikoi, from the Camp of Horse Artillery
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed the Crimean War camps around the village of Kadikoi. He could not photograph fighting, but his pictures showed people at home where soldiers lived.
photos.k: What would you pack for a camp like this?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed a busy wharf in the harbor of Balaklava, where ships brought guns and supplies for the army. The crowd of ships and crates shows how big the war effort was.
photos.k: What are the ships carrying?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed British and French soldiers together in the Crimea. The title means a friendly understanding, because the two countries fought on the same side.
photos.k: What kind of friendship does the picture suggest?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 22 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: British and French officers share a meal at a camp in Crimea. Fenton's pictures show a friendly side of war that newspapers wanted to see.
photos.k: What do you think they talked about?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 26 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed this British general during the Crimean War. Barnard was the chief of staff to the army and died soon after.
photos.k: What do you see in the way he stands?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Nadar photographed his friend Alexandre Dumas, who wrote The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo. Nadar's portraits caught the personality of writers and artists.
photos.k: What do you think a famous storyteller looks like?
photos.pr: salted paper print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: An amateur photographer, John Lloyd, photographed an older and a younger servant at a house in Wales. The picture shows two people who worked in a big house, side by side.
photos.k: How are the two different in age and in clothing?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Baldus photographed the old church at Auvers in France. Thirty years later, Vincent van Gogh would paint the same church in a famous painting.
photos.k: Have you seen Van Gogh's church? How is a photograph different from a painting?
photos.pr: salted paper print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Gift of Daniella Dangoor
photos.why: This stereograph shows a tall temple gateway, or gopura, in southern India. When you look at the two pictures with a viewer, the gateway seems to stand out in 3D.
photos.k: How could you make the picture seem 3D without a viewer?
photos.pr: stereoscopic albumen print from glass plate negative

photos.cr: Gift of William and Margaret Lipscomb
photos.why: Fenton photographed the young Lord Burghersh during his trip to the Crimea in 1855. He took portraits of the officers and their camps as part of a project for a publisher.
photos.k: Why would a publisher want pictures from the war?

photos.t: Louvre, Façade on the Rue de Rivoli
photos.cr: Gift of William and Margaret Lipscomb
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed the new Louvre façade in Paris in the 1850s. The government hired him to record its great new building projects.
photos.k: How is a photograph of a building different from the real building?

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed clouds in the sky, a hard thing to catch in the 1850s because the plates saw blue and white as the same. It is a rare early cloud study.
photos.k: What shapes do you see in the clouds?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed the railway yard at Balaklava during the Crimean War. A railway was built in weeks to carry supplies to the soldiers, and Fenton recorded the work.
photos.k: What do railway workers carry in a war?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed a post office in Balaklava. Letters from home were very important to soldiers, and this humble building was the place where they came.
photos.k: Why would letters matter so much to soldiers?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed the place where ships unloaded railway supplies. His pictures show war as a big logistics job, with piles of crates and cranes.
photos.k: What do you see being unloaded?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: This view shows the Ordnance Wharf at Balaklava, where guns and ammunition were landed. Fenton had to work quickly in the heat.
photos.k: What do you think the soldiers carried?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed the tents and horses of the Horse Artillery camp. A wagon served as his darkroom, and the heat often ruined his chemicals.
photos.k: Why would heat ruin photo chemicals?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed small stone cottages in the town of Balaklava during the Crimean War. Soldiers and officers used buildings like these as quarters.
photos.k: How might the soldiers have used these cottages?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.t: Mortar Batteries in Front of the Picquet House
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed rows of mortars, short guns that fired shells high into the air, near the front lines at Sevastopol. It is a picture of war made without any fighting in it.
photos.k: Why couldn't Fenton photograph the fighting?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed carts and cattle moving out of the port of Balaklava. Everything the army ate had to be carried by animals, and that makes the picture busy.
photos.k: What would you carry if you had to move an army?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed the besieged city of Sevastopol from a mortar battery. The battered city lies in the distance, beyond the soldiers' guns.
photos.k: What do you see in the distance?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed a house used by officers on a hill outside Sevastopol. Many of the buildings became the headquarters of soldiers.
photos.k: Why would an army choose a hill?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Admiral Lord Lyons commanded the British fleet in the Black Sea during the Crimean War. Fenton photographed him in 1855 beside a small tent.
photos.k: What does the admiral's uniform tell you?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed officers of a Scottish regiment, the 42nd Highlanders, in the Crimea. They wear kilts and tall feathered caps even in a war zone.
photos.k: Which part of the uniform seems the strangest for a war?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 17 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed a rough outdoor kitchen built by cavalry soldiers in the Crimea. Food was scarce and cold weather was harsh, and cooks did their best.
photos.k: What would you cook in a camp like this?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 51 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed the great cathedral of Amiens in France in a sweeping view. He pasted several negatives together to show the whole building.
photos.k: How could he fit such a tall building in one picture?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Hershey Family Art Purchase Fund
photos.why: You hardly ever see smiling portraits from the mid-1800s, because the sitter had to hold still and photographs were serious. This couple has a relaxed look, which makes it special.
photos.k: Why is it hard to smile for a long time?

photos.cr: Gift of Michael Mattis and Judith Hochberg
photos.why: Édouard Baldus photographed a new railway bridge over the Rhône river in Lyon. He documented rail projects across France, and his pictures show iron and stone engineering at its best.
photos.k: Why would a photographer be hired to photograph a bridge?

photos.cr: Hershey Family Art Purchase Fund
photos.why: A man poses on his own. The photographer let him choose a relaxed look, and his face seems to be on the edge of a smile.
photos.k: What would you do with your face for a portrait?

photos.cr: Purchase from the J. H. Wade Fund
photos.why: William Johnson photographed the entrance to the ancient Karli caves in western India in 1855. The caves are carved from solid rock and were used by Buddhist monks.
photos.k: How would you build a temple inside a mountain?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: A photographer in Hong Kong made this picture around 1855, perhaps a playful scene showing a trick or a gadget. Photography studios in China were some of the first in Asia.
photos.k: What do you think the device does?

photos.why: Charles Marville photographed the Bois de Boulogne, a huge park on the edge of Paris that was redesigned in the 1850s and 1860s. His pictures show a landscape that was newly made to look natural.
photos.k: What makes a park feel like nature?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Roger Fenton photographed the head of the harbor at Balaklava during the Crimean War, crowded with ships bringing supplies. Looking at it you can see how important the harbor was.
photos.k: How many ships can you count?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed the plateau above Sevastopol, where armies camped for a long siege. The empty, rocky ground is dotted with tents.
photos.k: What would living on a plateau in winter be like?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed the small port town of Balaklava from the heights. In 1855 it became a huge base for the British army.
photos.k: What do you notice about the shape of the harbor?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.t: Artillery Wagons, Balaklava in the Distance
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed wagons for the artillery with the harbor of Balaklava far behind. His war pictures show the logistics behind the fighting.
photos.k: What do the wagons carry?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Gift of Mrs. Everett Kovler
photos.why: Archibald Gordon was the chief medical officer for part of the British army in the Crimea. Fenton photographed doctors and officers.
photos.k: What would a doctor do in a war?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed a group of Croatian soldiers who fought for the Ottoman army in the Crimean War. Their colorful uniforms stand out in the camp.
photos.k: What details of their clothes can you see?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 2 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (18

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Photography and Media Purchase Fund
photos.why: Omar Pasha was the Ottoman general who fought the Russians in the Crimean War. Fenton photographed him in 1855 in the Crimea.
photos.k: What does a general's face show?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, plate 31 from the album "Photographs Taken in the Crimea" (1

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Alfred Rosling, a timber merchant and amateur photographer, photographed the harbor of Swansea in Wales. Fishing boats and cargo ships rest near the shore.
photos.k: What kinds of boats do you see?
photos.pr: albumen print from wax paper negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Léon-Eugène Méhédin photographed the Malakoff battery, a fort the French captured at Sevastopol in 1855. He worked as an official war photographer for the French army.
photos.k: Why is the fort so important?
photos.pr: varnished salt or albumen print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: A mother holds her child in this portrait from the mid-1850s. The photographer used the sunlight and soft pose to make the picture look like a painted Madonna.
photos.k: How does a mother hold a child so tenderly?

photos.t: Inclined Plane F, Delaware and Hudson Canal
photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Thomas H. Johnson made large photographs of the Delaware and Hudson Canal in the 1850s. Boats were pulled up a sloping track called an inclined plane.
photos.k: How would you move a boat uphill?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: Gift of Daniella Dangoor
photos.why: An unknown photographer showed a Hindu temple with its large water tank in Tamil Nadu in southern India. Tanks like these are used for ritual bathing.
photos.k: Why would a temple have a big pool?

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed ships returning to the French coast. He is famous for dramatic seascapes where sky and sea are both sharp.
photos.k: How do you think he made sky and sea both look right?

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed an old hollow oak in the forest of Fontainebleau. Painters and photographers loved the forest's ancient trees.
photos.k: How old do you think the tree is?

photos.why: The Getty Museum owns this photograph of the Taj Mahal from about 1855 to 1865 by Francis Frith. The great white marble tomb in Agra, India, was built by Shah Jahan for his wife.
photos.k: Why would an emperor build such a big tomb?

photos.why: Edward Bates was a lawyer from Missouri who became Abraham Lincoln's attorney general. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1850s.
photos.k: What does an attorney general do?

photos.why: Andrew Johnson, a tailor from Tennessee, became the 17th president of the United States after Lincoln's death. Mathew Brady photographed him in the 1850s.
photos.k: What would you look at in a future president's face?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: A sailing brig drifts on a calm sea beneath dramatic clouds. Gustave Le Gray was famous for seascapes like this, made by combining two negatives so both sea and sky looked right.
photos.k: What kind of weather does the sky suggest?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: The sun is a bright glow behind clouds and shines onto the sea. Le Gray was one of the first photographers to capture the sun's light directly, and people were amazed.
photos.k: Try to find where the sun reflects on the water.
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Elena Urschel; through prior gifts of Mr. Arnold Crane, David C. and Sarajean Ruttenberg, Max McGraw, and Reva and David Logan
photos.why: In 1856, the Rhône river flooded southern France. Édouard Baldus photographed fields turned into lakes, with trees and houses standing in the water.
photos.k: What would you do if your street became a river?

photos.cr: Julien Levy Collection, Gift of Jean and Julien Levy
photos.why: Gustave Doré was a French artist famous for illustrating the Bible and Dante's Inferno. Nadar, his friend, photographed him as a relaxed young man with a scarf.
photos.k: What do you think he drew in his sketchbook?

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Fenton photographed the sea at Cossack Bay near Balaklava during the Crimean War. He was one of the first to photograph a war zone, and this view is a quiet moment by the sea.
photos.k: What does a calm harbor in a war feel like?
photos.pr: Salted paper print, from the album "Photographic Pictures of the Seat of War in

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed the sea from a beach in Normandy. He was trained as a painter, and he found ways to show both the sky and the water in one picture.
photos.k: How are the sky and the sea different?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: Le Gray photographed the sun in the sky with a bright ring around it. To catch such a bright thing was a hard trick in 1856.
photos.k: Why is it so hard to photograph the sun?
photos.pr: Albumen print, No. 21 from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: Le Gray made some of the first beautiful seascapes. He joined two negatives, one for the sea and one for the sky, to get both right.
photos.k: How do you think he combined two pictures?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: Le Gray photographed a steamboat on the water in the 1850s. A boat moving through the water was a real challenge for early cameras.
photos.k: How do you think the ship stayed so sharp?
photos.pr: Albumen print, No. 3 from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Mayer and Pierson ran a studio in Paris that photographed famous and fashionable people. This portrait of a woman named Madame Carrelle shows a studio style that was copied everywhere.
photos.k: What do you notice about her dress?

photos.cr: Andrew R. and Martha Holden Jennings Fund
photos.why: Baldus photographed the new wing of the Louvre while workers were building it. The government wanted a record of its big project, and the photographs also showed how fine his sharp prints were.
photos.k: How many windows can you count?
photos.pr: salted paper print, albumenized, from wet collodion negative

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Richard Oakeley walked 20 days to photograph the carved temple at Halebidu in India. The stone walls are covered in tiny figures and gods, carved nearly 900 years ago.
photos.k: What kinds of figures can you find in the carvings?
photos.pr: albumenized salt print from waxed paper negative

photos.cr: Gift of Michael Mattis and Judith Hochberg
photos.why: Nadar photographed the Italian composer Rossini, who wrote the opera The Barber of Seville. Rossini finished 39 operas before he turned 39 and then mostly stopped.
photos.k: What would you do if you finished a big job at 39?

photos.cr: Dudley P. Allen Fund
photos.why: Henry White was a London lawyer and one of Britain's best landscape photographers in the 1850s. His fine pictures of trees and fields were praised at exhibitions.
photos.k: What do you see in the trees?
photos.pr: albumen print from wet collodion negative

photos.why: Gustave Le Gray photographed a sandy road climbing through the forest of Fontainebleau. The glowing path and dark trees make it look like a painting.
photos.k: Where do you think the path leads?

photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: Gustave Le Gray found a way to print both a dark sea and a bright, cloudy sky, which was almost impossible at the time. This steam tugboat on the horizon is one of his famous seascapes.
photos.k: What time of day do you think it is?
photos.pr: Albumen print, from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.why: Early film saw blue sky as white, so clouds almost disappeared. Gustave Le Gray found ways to print a dramatic cloudy sky, sometimes using a separate negative, and made some of the first great sky pictures.
photos.k: What shapes can you see in the clouds?

photos.t: The Dome of the Rock, Jerusalem
photos.why: The golden Dome of the Rock has shone over Jerusalem for more than 1,300 years. Felix Beato photographed the city from the Mount of Olives side, with the old walls in front.
photos.k: Find the dome. What do you notice about the wall in front?

photos.t: Ships in the Harbor at Sète
photos.cr: Hugh Edwards Fund
photos.why: Tall masts and rigging fill a French Mediterranean harbor. Le Gray made the ships crisp and the sky soft, so the picture feels almost like a painting.
photos.k: How many masts can you count?
photos.pr: Albumen print, No. 10 from the album "Vistas del Mar"

photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
photos.why: Francis Frith carried a wagon-sized darkroom up the Nile and photographed ancient temples. A few columns remain standing here in the sunny sand.
photos.k: What happened to the rest of the temple?
photos.pr: Albumen print, pl. 5 from the album "Egypt and Palestine, Volume I" (1858)

photos.t: Osiride Pillars and the Fallen Colossus
photos.cr: Photography Gallery Fund
