photos.why: Doris Ulmann photographed the dancer Ruth St. Denis around 1925. St. Denis helped found modern dance in the United States.
photos.k: How do dancers tell stories without words?

photos.why: Imogen Cunningham photographed two calla lilies in 1925. The simple shapes and sharp light make the flowers look like sculpture.
photos.k: How are the two flowers different?

photos.why: Roger Dumas made an autochrome of the Polish delegation at the Locarno Conference in 1925. Men in dark coats stand in a garden.
photos.k: What would you wear to an important meeting?

photos.why: Roger Dumas made an autochrome of the German delegation at Locarno in 1925. Germany joined the agreements to keep peace in Europe.
photos.k: Why would former enemies sign agreements?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon C. Abbott photographed fields and farmland in Mexico in 1925. The picture shows how people worked the land, with hills in the distance.
photos.k: What crops do you think grew here?

photos.t: Still Life with Lemons and a Siphon
photos.why: Emmanuel Sougez photographed lemons, a blue soda siphon and printed paper on a table. In the 1920s, photographers began to see ordinary objects as pure shapes and colors.
photos.k: What shapes can you find in the arrangement?

photos.why: Eugène Atget photographed a hairdresser's window in Paris full of mannequin heads in wigs. The Surrealist artists loved this picture because it looks strange and dreamlike.
photos.k: Why does a window full of heads feel odd?

photos.cr: Gift of David C. and Sarajean Ruttenberg
photos.why: Lewis Hine photographed an elderly Jewish immigrant woman at Ellis Island, where millions of newcomers entered America. Hine's portraits showed the dignity of people arriving with little.
photos.k: What do you think she was feeling?

photos.why: Underwood and Underwood photographed the old sailing ship USS Constellation at Newport, Rhode Island, in 1926. The wooden warship, launched in 1854, was used as a training ship.
photos.k: How is a sailing ship different from a modern one?

photos.cr: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz and Georgia O'Keeffe lived high in the Shelton Hotel in New York. From their window, Stieglitz photographed the growing skyscrapers and factory chimneys beyond.
photos.k: What would it be like to look out over the city from so high?

photos.why: Bảo Đại became the emperor of Annam, in what is now Vietnam, as a boy. This color portrait shows him in a dark outfit and cap, as a teenager preparing to rule.
photos.k: What would it be like to be an emperor as a teenager?

photos.why: Paul von Hindenburg was a German general and then president of Germany. This color autochrome from a German magazine shows him in a dark suit with a medal.
photos.k: What do you notice about his face and moustache?

photos.why: Albert Kahn's photographers took color pictures of people all over the world. These two men from the Bahdinan Kurds, in colorful clothes, were photographed on glass plates.
photos.k: Which parts of their clothing do you find most colorful?

photos.t: Charles Lindbergh and the Spirit of St. Louis
photos.why: In May 1927, Charles Lindbergh flew alone, without stopping, from New York to Paris in a small plane called the Spirit of St. Louis. The flight took thirty-three and a half hours and made him the most famous person in the world.
photos.k: How would you stay awake for thirty-three hours?

photos.cr: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed Dorothy Norman, a young photographer and writer who became his close friend. He made many portraits of her in the late 1920s and early 1930s.
photos.k: Why would a photographer photograph someone again and again?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Jaromír Funke was a Czech photographer who made abstract pictures from everyday objects in the 1920s. He arranged glass, shadows and light into shapes.
photos.k: What everyday things can you find in the picture?
photos.pr: gelatin silver print, silver bromide, photogram

photos.why: Edward S. Curtis photographed a man wearing a ceremonial mask in Nunivak, an island off the coast of Alaska, in 1927. The masks were used in dances and stories.
photos.k: What story would a mask tell?

photos.why: Edward S. Curtis photographed two men in hooded parkas landing their kayaks at the village of Noatak in Alaska in 1927. They had to be dressed for the cold.
photos.k: How do you stay warm in a kayak?

photos.why: Georges Chevalier photographed Ali Fethi Bey, the ambassador of Turkey, in 1927. Fethi was one of the first prime ministers of the Republic of Turkey.
photos.k: What does an ambassador do?

photos.t: Distortograph of Mayor William Hale Thompson
photos.why: Herbert Ponting invented a machine called a Distortograph that made funny, stretched pictures. This one shows Chicago's Mayor Big Bill Thompson.
photos.k: What would your face look like in a funhouse mirror?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: This photograph from a flood album shows the St. Francis River near Trumann, Arkansas, during the great Mississippi flood of 1927. Water spread over farms and towns.
photos.k: What would you do if your house was flooded?

photos.t: Photographers on a Platform at Lindbergh's Welcome
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Photographers stand on a platform above the crowd to take pictures of Charles Lindbergh's welcome in Washington in June 1927. A few weeks earlier he had flown alone across the Atlantic.
photos.k: Why would everyone want a photograph of Lindbergh?

photos.t: Crowd on the Washington Monument Grounds to Welcome Lindbergh
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Crowds gathered on the Washington Monument grounds on June 11, 1927, to welcome Charles Lindbergh. He had flown nonstop from New York to Paris in the Spirit of St. Louis.
photos.k: Why was a solo flight across an ocean so amazing?

photos.why: Edward Steichen became chief photographer for Vogue and Vanity Fair in the 1920s. He photographed this actress in the sleek Art Deco style.
photos.k: How would you pose to look glamorous?

photos.t: An Inupiat Family from Noatak, Alaska
photos.why: Edward Curtis photographed an Inupiat family in thick fur parkas on his trips to Alaska in the late 1920s. A mother and father look at the camera, with a baby peeking out from the furs.
photos.k: How do you think fur keeps people warm in the Arctic?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed the Irish writer James Joyce in Paris in 1928. Joyce wrote Ulysses, a famous novel, and he was nearly blind by then.
photos.k: What would you ask a writer of such a long novel?

photos.why: Karl Blossfeldt photographed an acanthus plant in 1928 close up, showing the shape of the leaf. He taught art in Berlin and used the pictures to show students how plants make forms.
photos.k: Which shape in the plant looks like architecture?

photos.why: Karl Blossfeldt photographed a plant from the squash family, called Cucurbita, in 1928. He built simple cameras to magnify plants up to 30 times.
photos.k: How does magnifying a plant change it?

photos.t: Vogue Fashion Photographs with Model Gurta Andre
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Arnold Genthe photographed the model Gurta Andre in 1928 for Vogue. He was a society photographer and made portraits of fashion models.
photos.k: How are fashion pictures different from portraits?

photos.why: Walker Evans was a young photographer in 1929, finding beauty in plain things around him. In this early picture, a woman walks on a boardwalk in a summer dress.
photos.k: What season does it feel like?

photos.why: Man Ray photographed Victoria Ocampo, an Argentine writer, in 1929 in a dress by Chanel. Ocampo founded a famous literary magazine, Sur.
photos.k: What would it be like to publish a magazine?

photos.why: This photograph from Karl Blossfeldt's 1928 book Urformen der Kunst, Art Forms in Nature, shows a plant stem magnified. The book became a bestseller and changed how people looked at plants.
photos.k: What does the plant remind you of?

photos.why: Margaret Bourke-White photographed the Otis Steel mill in Cleveland, Ohio, in 1929 for Fortune magazine. Her picture of the glowing furnaces made her famous as a photographer of industry.
photos.k: How can a factory seem dramatic?

photos.why: Doris Ulmann photographed a prison work crew digging a trench with a guard watching in the South in the 1920s. Prisoners often did road work.
photos.k: What would working on a crew be like?

photos.why: Imogen Cunningham photographed a hen and her chicks in 1929. She loved plants and animals, and her sharp, clean pictures were praised.
photos.k: How do you hold chicks safely?

photos.why: Imogen Cunningham photographed a leaf pattern in 1929. She made plants look like sculptures by choosing sharp focus and strong light.
photos.k: What shapes do the veins of leaves make?

photos.why: Edward S. Curtis photographed an Inuit man in a kayak around 1929 at Noatak, Alaska. The kayak is a boat made from skins stretched over a frame.
photos.k: Why would a boat made from skin be good in cold water?

photos.t: Crowd with Washington Monument in the Background
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Harris and Ewing photographed a crowd at the Washington Monument in 1929. Washington crowds gathered for parades and speeches.
photos.k: What event do you think the crowd came to see?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jacob Gayer photographed sugarcane harvesting at Central Romana in the Dominican Republic in 1929. Cane workers cut the tall stalks with machetes.
photos.k: How would you cut tall stalks of cane?

photos.t: From My Window at An American Place, North
photos.cr: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
photos.why: Stieglitz photographed the New York skyline from the window of his gallery. Tall buildings crowd the sky in a hazy gray, as New York grew upward.
photos.k: How many skyscrapers can you count?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Lewis Hine climbed the Empire State Building as it was built to photograph workers high above New York. Here a man works on the mast with a flag as the city spreads out below.
photos.k: Would you be brave enough to work up there?

photos.t: Derrick Worker on the Empire State Building
photos.cr: Gift of Robert A. Taub
photos.why: Lewis Hine photographed a worker on a derrick high on the Empire State Building in 1930. Hine climbed up with the workers to take his pictures.
photos.k: Would you work on a skyscraper?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed Midtown Manhattan at night from the top of a building around 1930. The glow of lit towers made the city look like a sparkling forest.
photos.k: What does a city look like from far above at night?

photos.why: Man Ray photographed the French poet Louis Aragon around 1930. Aragon was a founder of the Surrealist movement.
photos.k: What is surrealism?

photos.t: Arcady, Where All the Leaves Are Merry
photos.why: Frances Benjamin Johnston photographed a garden scene in 1930 titled Arcady, after a line of poetry. She was a leading architectural and garden photographer.
photos.k: Why would someone name a garden Arcady?

photos.t: Aerial View of the Fremantle War Memorial
photos.why: Frank Hurley photographed the war memorial in Fremantle, Western Australia, from the air in 1930. He was fond of airplane photographs.
photos.k: What does a memorial look like from above?

photos.why: Edward Weston photographed a halved artichoke in 1930. He found sculptural shapes in vegetables, and the overlapping leaves make graceful patterns.
photos.k: What shapes do you see inside the artichoke?

photos.t: Tugboat Frank W. on the Cuyahoga River
photos.why: Margaret Bourke-White photographed the tugboat Frank W. pulling a boat on the Cuyahoga River in Cleveland in 1929. The river was the center of the city's steel industry.
photos.k: What does a tugboat do?

photos.t: Girl Athletes at a Pre-Olympic Night Sports Festival
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Girl athletes take part in a night sports festival before the Olympics in 1930. Women's sports were growing quickly.
photos.k: What sport would you like to try at night?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A railroad conductor and an engineer pose beside a train in 1930. The conductor checks tickets and the engineer drives the locomotive.
photos.k: Who would you rather be?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: The American Red Cross photographed a family of nine sharing a small home in 1930 during the early Depression. Families doubled up during hard times.
photos.k: How would you share a small room with eight people?

photos.t: Georgia O'Keeffe: Hands and Horse Skull
photos.cr: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed O'Keeffe's hands as she held a horse skull she had brought back from New Mexico. She painted bones and skulls of the desert as symbols of beauty.
photos.k: Why would a painter love a bone?

photos.t: Climbing Up the Beams on the Empire State Building
photos.cr: The Mary and Leigh Block Endowment Fund
photos.why: Lewis Hine climbed the steel frame of the Empire State Building as it rose in 1930 and 1931. He photographed the builders from dizzying angles, showing ordinary workers as heroes.
photos.k: Would you want to work this high above the ground?

photos.why: Edward Weston photographed a cabbage leaf in 1931 and made the wavy edges look like a sculpture. He used a small aperture to get everything sharp.
photos.k: What does the leaf look like besides a cabbage?

photos.why: Skyscrapers, including the shining top of the Chrysler Building, rise above the streets of Manhattan. By 1932 New York had more tall buildings than any other city in the world.
photos.k: Which building do you think is the tallest?

photos.why: Eleven men eat lunch while sitting on a steel beam hundreds of feet above New York in 1932. The picture, probably staged as publicity for Rockefeller Center, shows the daring of the ironworkers who built the city's skyscrapers.
photos.k: How would you feel sitting on that beam?

photos.cr: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed Dorothy Norman in 1932 with a double portrait. His series of her face and hands became a major work.
photos.k: What can you show with a double photograph?

photos.t: From My Window at An American Place, Southwest
photos.cr: Alfred Stieglitz Collection
photos.why: Alfred Stieglitz photographed the New York skyline from his gallery window, An American Place, in 1932. He photographed the view in all weather for years.
photos.k: What changes when you look at the same view every day?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Pierre Dubreuil made a carefully planned still life from ordinary objects in 1932. It is part of his modernist way of arranging common things.
photos.k: What ordinary things can you spot?
photos.pr: oil print, Rawlins oil print process

photos.why: Imogen Cunningham photographed the young actor Cary Grant in 1932. She took portraits of celebrities for Vanity Fair.
photos.k: What makes a movie star look like one?

photos.why: Lotte Jacobi photographed Ernst Thälmann, a German Communist leader, around 1932. Jacobi was a German photographer who fled the Nazis.
photos.k: Why would a photographer have to flee?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Members of the American bobsled team pose at Lake Placid, New York, in 1932 for the Winter Olympics. Bobsleds race down an icy track.
photos.k: Would you ride a bobsled?

photos.t: Betty Robinson Trains for a Comeback
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Betty Robinson, the first female Olympic champion in track and field, won the 100-meter dash in 1928. After a plane crash in 1931 she trained to run again.
photos.k: How does someone recover from a bad injury?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Betty Robinson discards the crutches she needed after a plane crash. She went on to win a gold medal in the 1936 relay.
photos.k: What gives someone courage to try again?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Mildred Babe Didrikson was a star in track and field, basketball and golf. She won two gold medals and a silver at the 1932 Olympics in Los Angeles, and she later became a champion golfer.
photos.k: Which sport would you try first?

photos.why: Walker Evans photographed the streets of Havana, Cuba, from a rooftop. The picture shows a great square courtyard of apartments and shops, almost like a map.
photos.k: What can you tell about how people lived from this view?

photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed Glacier National Park in Montana for the National Park Service between 1933 and 1942. His crisp black-and-white pictures made the mountains look huge.
photos.k: How does black-and-white make mountains look strong?

photos.t: St. Mary's Lake, Glacier National Park
photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed St. Mary Lake in Glacier National Park in Montana. Dark mountains frame the still, silvery water.
photos.k: What do the mountains do to the lake?

photos.t: Two Medicine Lake, Glacier National Park
photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed Two Medicine Lake in Glacier National Park. The lake lies below sharp peaks in a quiet valley.
photos.k: What would you hear at a lake in the mountains?

photos.t: Schoolchildren Line Up for Free Lunch
photos.why: During the Great Depression many families had little money for food, and schoolchildren lined up for free meals. Photographers recorded these scenes to show how hard times were.
photos.k: How would you feel if you had to line up for lunch like this?

photos.why: Carl Van Vechten photographed the writer Gertrude Stein in New York in 1934, when she visited the United States on a lecture tour. Stein wore a vest and her hair short.
photos.k: Why would a lecture tour be exciting?

photos.why: Tall chimneys and furnaces rise over the town of Port Pirie, in South Australia, where metals from mines were smelted. Frank Hurley, the explorer-photographer, photographed Australia's industries.
photos.k: What do you think comes out of those chimneys?

photos.why: A bright painted circus poster covers a wall in Alabama. Walker Evans photographed signs and posters across the country as a kind of folk art, and the colors burst through even in black and white.
photos.k: Which performers do you see on the poster?

photos.why: Rows of workers' houses climb the hill under the stacks of a huge steel mill. Walker Evans photographed American towns in the Depression for a government project, and this one is one of his best-known views.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a house in the shadow of a mill?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed the west side of Gramercy Park in Manhattan in 1935 for her Changing New York project. The old brownstones stand around a private park.
photos.k: Why is it special to live around a private park?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed Mulberry and Prince Streets in Manhattan in 1935 for Changing New York. An old building with a gambrel roof stands among new tenements.
photos.k: What kinds of buildings do you see?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed fish dealers and the Meyers Hotel on South Street in Manhattan in 1935. The old Fulton Fish Market was one of the busiest in the country.
photos.k: What smells would you notice?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed First Avenue and East 70th Street in Manhattan in 1935. Shops and apartments in older buildings line the street.
photos.k: What changes in a city over time?

photos.why: Underwood and Underwood photographed the boxer Joe Louis in 1935, the year he became a national hero. He later held the heavyweight title for nearly twelve years.
photos.k: What makes a champion?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Carl Mydans photographed children playing in a Washington, D.C., street in 1935 for the Resettlement Administration. The pictures showed daily life during the Depression.
photos.k: What games do you play outside?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Carl Mydans photographed the train station at Radburn, New Jersey, a planned community built in the 1920s. Radburn was designed with parks and separate roads for cars and walkers.
photos.k: Why would a planner separate cars from people?

photos.t: Dust Storm near Mills, New Mexico
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Dorothea Lange photographed a dust storm near Mills, New Mexico, in 1935 for the government. In the 1930s, drought turned the plains into a dust bowl.
photos.k: What would a dust storm be like?

photos.cr: Gift of David Vestal
photos.why: People crowd around a table to collect checks from a government program that helped unemployed workers during the Great Depression. Lewis Hine photographed the New Deal at work.
photos.k: Why would people need help like this?

photos.cr: Purchased with funds provided by Mrs. James Ward Thorne
photos.why: A studio window in Savannah, Georgia, shows rows of small cheap portraits of local people. Walker Evans loved photographs by ordinary people, and he copied the look of studio displays in his own work.
photos.k: If you could see just one face here, which would you choose?

photos.why: Walker Evans traveled to Alabama with the writer James Agee in 1936 to document the lives of tenant farmers. This small wooden cabin is among the pictures from that trip.
photos.k: What does the cabin look like inside?

photos.why: Allie Mae Burroughs was a young cotton farmer's wife in Alabama, photographed by Walker Evans. She looks straight at the camera with a calm, tired face. The picture is one of the best-known portraits of the Depression.
photos.k: What do you think her life was like?

photos.t: Farmer Walking in a Dust Storm
photos.why: A farmer crosses his yard in Cimarron County, Oklahoma, as a dust storm blows. In the 1930s, drought and wind turned the Great Plains into a Dust Bowl. Arthur Rothstein photographed the storms for the government.
photos.k: What would happen to a crop in a dust storm?

photos.why: In March 1936, Dorothea Lange stopped at a camp of pea pickers in California and photographed a woman named Florence Owens Thompson with her children. The photograph went to newspapers, and food was sent to the camp. It became the most famous image of the Great Depression.
photos.k: What do you see in the mother's face?

photos.why: Two children crouch in the street playing a game, as photographed by Russell Lee. He photographed small-town life across the US for a government project during the Depression.
photos.k: What kind of game do you think they were playing?

photos.why: Shelves of tin cans, flour sacks and cloth fill a country store in Alabama. Walker Evans photographed the things people used every day, as a record of a time.
photos.k: What can you find to buy in this store?

photos.why: Jagged peaks rise above a barren slope in California's Sierra Nevada. Ansel Adams photographed this region in 1936 for the Sierra Club, whose campaign helped to create Kings Canyon National Park.
photos.k: How would you climb up those peaks?

photos.why: Bud Fields was a cotton farmer in Hale County, Alabama. Walker Evans photographed him and his family for the book Let Us Now Praise Famous Men, to show the dignity of people living through hard times.
photos.k: What can you see in his face?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed New York for years to record how fast it was changing. She looked down on this canyon of skyscrapers in the Financial District from above, so the buildings tower and cross like angled walls.
photos.k: How does the high viewpoint make the buildings look?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A wall of dust blows over a farm in Oklahoma in 1936. Dust storms like this carried topsoil hundreds of miles and forced many families to leave their farms.
photos.k: How would you protect a house from dust?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Drifts of dust bury fences and cover a farm. After years without rain, the soil blew away, leaving farmers with nothing to grow.
photos.k: How would you clean up after a storm like this?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed Cedar Street in Lower Manhattan in 1936 for Changing New York. Tall buildings line a narrow canyon.
photos.k: How does a street look at the bottom of skyscrapers?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed Broadway and Thomas Street from above in 1936 for Changing New York. Looking down shows the traffic and people.
photos.k: What do you see from high above a street?

photos.why: Edward Weston photographed the sand dunes at Oceano, California, in 1936. The curves look like the shapes of bodies, and the light makes strong ridges.
photos.k: What shapes does the wind make in sand?

photos.t: Custom House Statue behind the New York Produce Exchange
photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed two statues behind the New York Produce Exchange building in 1936. The old buildings in Lower Manhattan were being torn down.
photos.k: What happens to old statues when a building is torn down?

photos.t: Burroughs Children Playing in the Yard
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Walker Evans photographed the children of the Burroughs family in Hale County, Alabama, in 1936. He was working for Fortune magazine with the writer James Agee, who wrote about tenant farm families.
photos.k: What games do you play in the yard?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Dorothea Lange photographed a migrant camp in California in 1936. Families who had lost farms in the Dust Bowl lived in tents and cars.
photos.k: What would you pack if you had to leave home?

photos.t: Woman Sharecropper near West Memphis, Arkansas
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Carl Mydans photographed an African American woman sharecropper near West Memphis, Arkansas, in 1936. Sharecroppers farmed land owned by others and shared the crop with the landlord.
photos.k: Why was sharecropping a hard life?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Carl Mydans photographed a sharecropper's shack near West Memphis, Arkansas, in 1936. The wood house is small and weathered.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a place like this?

photos.t: Opening of the Garment Factory, Hightstown, New Jersey
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Carl Mydans photographed the opening of a garment factory in Hightstown, New Jersey, in 1936. It was part of a government plan to move families to a new town called Jersey Homesteads.
photos.k: What would you make in a factory?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Carl Mydans photographed a farm in Pennsylvania in 1936 for the Resettlement Administration. The agency studied farms to see how to help farmers.
photos.k: How would you improve a farm?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Walker Evans photographed a small church in South Carolina in 1936. He loved plain buildings and photographed them straight on.
photos.k: What do you notice about the church's simple shape?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Walker Evans photographed a church in St. Marys, Georgia, in 1936. His clear, straight-on pictures of buildings became a model for later photographers.
photos.k: How does a straight-on photograph feel?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Walker Evans photographed a simple grave in Hale County, Alabama, in 1936. The grave is marked by a mound of earth and a few objects.
photos.k: What does a simple grave say about a person?

photos.t: Kitchen Corner in an Alabama Tenant Farmer's House
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Walker Evans photographed a corner of a tenant farmer's kitchen in Alabama in 1936, with shelves and plain dishes. His pictures show poverty and dignity.
photos.k: What can you learn from a kitchen?

photos.cr: Gift of Robert A. Taub
photos.why: Hands guide stockings through a machine in a factory. Lewis Hine photographed workers' hands and skills to show that modern industry depended on the people who ran the machines.
photos.k: What do you notice about the hands in this picture?

photos.t: Broke, Baby Sick, and Car Trouble!
photos.why: Dorothea Lange wrote down what people told her, and this family's own words became her title. Their car, loaded with belongings, broke down on a California highway as they searched for work during the Depression.
photos.k: What would you do if your car broke down far from home?

photos.why: On May 6, 1937, the German airship Hindenburg burst into flames as it landed in Lakehurst, New Jersey, killing 36 people. Photographers like Sam Shere were waiting for the landing, and these pictures ended the age of giant passenger airships.
photos.k: Why do you think airships don't carry passengers today?

photos.why: Carl Van Vechten photographed the composer George Gershwin in 1937. Gershwin wrote Rhapsody in Blue and the opera Porgy and Bess.
photos.k: What would you do if you wrote music like Rhapsody in Blue?

photos.t: Frida Kahlo Seated Next to an Agave
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed the Mexican painter Frida Kahlo seated beside an agave plant in 1937. Kahlo's self-portraits are famous around the world.
photos.k: How would you pose with a plant?

photos.t: Firehouse, Park Avenue and East 135th Street
photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed an old wooden firehouse in Harlem in 1937. The little two-story shingled building stood among larger ones.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a firehouse?

photos.t: Francis Townsend Speaking at a Club
photos.why: Dr. Francis Townsend speaks to a club in 1937. He proposed a pension plan for older Americans during the Great Depression that led to Social Security.
photos.k: Why is a pension for older people a good idea?

photos.why: A photograph for the Historic American Buildings Survey shows the blacksmith shop at Ringwood Manor in New Jersey in 1937. The Survey hired photographers during the Depression to record old buildings.
photos.k: What would a blacksmith make?

photos.why: Josiah Tubby photographed the Harpswell Meetinghouse in Maine in 1937 for the Historic American Buildings Survey. The plain church dates from 1757.
photos.k: Why would a village have a plain meetinghouse?

photos.why: Lotte Jacobi photographed Albert Einstein in 1937, a few years after he moved to the United States. Einstein gave her several sittings.
photos.k: What would you ask a great scientist?

photos.t: Migrant Agricultural Worker near Holtville, California
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Dorothea Lange photographed a migrant farm worker near Holtville, California, in 1937. Many workers followed the crops from one place to another.
photos.k: How would you live if you moved with the harvest?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Dorothea Lange photographed the home of migrant farmworkers in California in 1937, a shack with a patchwork roof. Housing for field workers was poor.
photos.k: What would you use to patch a roof?

photos.why: Berenice Abbott photographed New York for years to record how fast it was changing. This hardware store spills pails, paints and tools onto the sidewalk and shows how a shop looked in the 1930s.
photos.k: What tools do you recognize?

photos.t: Doorway of the Reverend Ebenezer Gay House, Suffield
photos.why: Everett Keeler photographed the carved doorway of an 1700s house in Suffield, Connecticut, in 1938. The doorway has a broken pediment, a style typical of colonial homes.
photos.k: What do you see in the doorway's carving?

photos.t: Einstein and Infeld Writing a Book
photos.why: Lotte Jacobi photographed Albert Einstein and Leopold Infeld in 1938 writing The Evolution of Physics. The two scientists wrote a book to explain modern physics to readers.
photos.k: How would you explain a hard idea?

photos.why: Edward Weston photographed the surf at China Cove at Point Lobos, California, in 1938. The waves crash against rocks and curve like ribbons.
photos.k: How does the water move around the rocks?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed a Methodist church in Urbana, Ohio, in 1938 for the Farm Security Administration. A simple white building with a spire sits on a street corner.
photos.k: Why do small towns often have a church in the middle?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed people leaving church in Linworth, Ohio, in 1938. They are in their Sunday best.
photos.k: What do you wear to special events?

photos.t: The Thaxton Family, near Mechanicsburg, Ohio
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed the Thaxton family near Mechanicsburg, Ohio, in 1938 for the Farm Security Administration. Shahn was also a painter and noticed faces and clothes.
photos.k: What does the family's clothing tell you?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed the main street of Plain City, Ohio, in 1938. Cars and low brick buildings line the street.
photos.k: What would you find on a main street in a small town?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed the bus station in Marion, Ohio, in 1938. Buses connected small towns to cities.
photos.k: What would it be like to wait for a bus then?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed a family on relief in Lancaster, Ohio, in 1938. Relief meant help from the government for families who had no work.
photos.k: How can a government help families in hard times?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed workers eating dinner during the wheat harvest in central Ohio in 1938. Neighboring farmers helped each other, and a big meal fed the crew.
photos.k: What would you cook for harvest workers?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Ben Shahn photographed a family in Marysville, Ohio, in 1938. His pictures were used by the Farm Security Administration to show how Americans lived.
photos.k: How can a photograph show how a family lives?

photos.t: Blowing Dust in the Oklahoma Panhandle
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Dorothea Lange photographed blowing dust in the Oklahoma Panhandle in 1938. Clouds of dust covered farms during the Dust Bowl.
photos.k: What would you do in a dust storm?

photos.why: A barber trims a customer's hair on a porch in a Mississippi town while other men wait. Marion Post Wolcott photographed daily life in the Deep South for the government.
photos.k: Would you want a haircut outdoors?

photos.t: Loaders at the Pillsbury Flour Mill, Minneapolis
photos.why: John Vachon photographed loaders at the Pillsbury flour mill in Minneapolis in 1939. Minneapolis was known as the Mill City because it made so much flour.
photos.k: How would you move sacks of flour?

photos.t: Tyrone Power and Annabella After Their Wedding
photos.why: The Los Angeles Times photographed the film stars Tyrone Power and Annabella after their wedding in Bel Air in April 1939. Movie weddings drew crowds of fans.
photos.k: Why would people want to see a movie star's wedding?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Dorothea Lange photographed a migrant worker in a camp in California in 1939. Families lived in tents and cars near the fields.
photos.k: What would you miss about home?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed commuters who had just come off a train and were waiting for a bus in 1939. Commuting to work was part of daily life in New England.
photos.k: How do you get to school or work?

photos.t: Railroad Cars and Factory Buildings, Lawrence, Massachusetts
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed railroad cars and factory buildings in Lawrence, Massachusetts, in 1939. The city was famous for its textile mills.
photos.k: What were the mills making?

photos.t: Detail of an Industrial Building in Massachusetts
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed the brick and windows of a factory building in Massachusetts in 1939 for the Farm Security Administration. The repeating windows make a pattern against the sky.
photos.k: How many windows can you count?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a street in Mystic, Connecticut, in 1939. The seaport town was known for shipbuilding.
photos.k: What would you see on a main street in a port town?

photos.t: Children with an Adult in the Tenement District, Brockton, Massachusetts
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed children and an adult in a crowded neighborhood in Brockton, Massachusetts, in 1939. Brockton was a shoe-making city, and many workers lived in tenements.
photos.k: What would it be like to live in a crowded neighborhood?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed the Douglas shoe factory in Brockton in 1939. Brockton produced more shoes than any other city in the United States.
photos.k: How many shoes would a factory make in a day?

photos.t: Copper Mining and Sulfuric Acid Plant, Copperhill, Tennessee
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed a copper mine and sulfuric acid plant at Copperhill, Tennessee, in 1939. The fumes from the smelters had killed the plants on the hills around.
photos.k: How can factories change the land around them?

photos.t: A Train Bringing Copper Ore from the Mine, Ducktown, Tennessee
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed a train carrying copper ore out of the mines at Ducktown, Tennessee, in 1939. Mining here began in the 1840s.
photos.k: What is copper used for?

photos.t: Black Tenant's Home beside the Mississippi River Levee
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed the home of a Black tenant farmer by the Mississippi River levee in 1939. Levees are high banks that protect fields from floods.
photos.k: How would you feel living next to a levee?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed Bayou Bourbeau, a farm cooperative in Louisiana, in 1939. The Farm Security Administration helped farmers pool resources.
photos.k: What does it mean to work in a cooperative?

photos.t: Fishing in a Creek near Cotton Plantations
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed Black people fishing in a creek outside Belzoni, Mississippi, in 1939. Fishing brought food and a break from field work.
photos.k: What would you catch in a creek?

photos.t: Going to Town on Saturday Afternoon, Greene County, Georgia
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a family going to town in a wagon in Greene County, Georgia, in 1939. Saturday was the day rural families went to shop and meet friends.
photos.k: What would you do in town on Saturday?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed workers chopping cotton on rented land near White Plains in Greene County, Georgia, in 1939. Chopping means thinning the rows of cotton by hoe.
photos.k: Why is chopping cotton hard work?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Russell Lee photographed grain elevators in Caldwell, Idaho, in 1939. These tall storage buildings hold the harvest of local farms.
photos.k: Why would grain need to be stored high?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Russell Lee photographed a flour mill in Caldwell, Idaho, in 1939. Mills turn wheat into flour.
photos.k: How is wheat turned into flour?

photos.t: Cherry Orchards and Farming Land, Emmett, Idaho
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Russell Lee photographed orchards in Emmett, Idaho, in 1939. Irrigation from the river turned the dry valley into farmland.
photos.k: Why do orchards need irrigation?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Russell Lee photographed the main street of Cascade, Idaho, in 1939. The small mountain town sits by a reservoir in the Salmon River country.
photos.k: What would shops on a mountain street sell?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Russell Lee photographed a wheat farm near Walla Walla, Washington, in 1939. Rolling hills are planted with golden wheat.
photos.k: What does a wheat field look like in the wind?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Russell Lee photographed a pea cannery in Milton-Freewater, Oregon, in 1939. Peas were a main crop in the valley.
photos.k: How do you get peas into a can?

photos.t: Parachute Instructor, Meacham Field, Fort Worth
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Arthur Rothstein photographed an instructor explaining a parachute to students at Meacham Field in Fort Worth, Texas, in 1939. A civilian pilot training program prepared pilots before the war.
photos.k: Would you want to learn to fly?

photos.t: Student Pilots, Meacham Field, Fort Worth
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Arthur Rothstein photographed student pilots at Meacham Field, Fort Worth, Texas, in 1939. The government paid for civilian flying lessons.
photos.k: What would you learn first as a pilot?

photos.t: Civilian Pilot Training School, Returning from Practice Flight
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Student pilots walk back from a practice flight at Meacham Field, Fort Worth, in 1939. Planes in the background sit on the field.
photos.k: What would you feel after your first flight?

photos.t: Instructor and Students Studying a Map
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Arthur Rothstein photographed an instructor and students studying a map at Meacham Field in 1939. Pilots had to learn to navigate.
photos.k: How would you find your way in the sky?

photos.t: Families of Migratory Workers in Front of Row Shelters
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Arthur Rothstein photographed families of migratory workers in front of their row shelters at a Farm Security Administration camp in Robstown, Texas, in 1939. The camps gave workers decent places to live.
photos.k: Why would a camp be better than living in a car?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Arthur Rothstein photographed boys playing marbles at a labor camp in Robstown, Texas, in 1939. Kids still found games in hard times.
photos.k: How do you play marbles?

photos.t: Gardens in Front of the Row Shelters
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Residents of the Robstown labor camp planted gardens in front of the row shelters in 1939. The government camp encouraged gardening.
photos.k: What would you plant outside your home?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Collier photographed a worker cultivating a field at Seabrook Farm in Bridgeton, New Jersey, in 1939. Seabrook was one of the biggest vegetable farms in America.
photos.k: How do you cultivate a field?

photos.t: Bean Field and Canning Factory, Seabrook Farm
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Collier photographed a bean field next to a canning factory at Seabrook Farm in 1939. The farm and factory were joined for freezing and canning vegetables.
photos.k: Why build a factory right next to the field?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Collier photographed day laborers, some from nearby towns and others migrants, picking string beans at Seabrook Farm in 1939. They worked from early morning.
photos.k: How many beans would you pick in a day?

photos.t: Low-Flying Plane Spreading Dust or Insecticide
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Collier photographed a low-flying plane spreading dust or insecticide over crops at Seabrook Farm in 1939. Crop dusting was new, and planes covered fields quickly.
photos.k: Why would a farmer use a plane?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed a shot putter at the University of Nebraska around 1939. Track and field was a big sport at Midwest colleges.
photos.k: What does a shot put weigh?

photos.t: Girl with Doll by a Fence
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A girl stands by a fence holding her doll in a rural scene from the late 1930s. The photograph was made for the Farm Security Administration.
photos.k: What would you do with a doll in a field?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A field of sunflowers stands tall in a photograph from the Farm Security Administration around 1939. Sunflowers turn to face the sun.
photos.k: Why do sunflowers follow the sun?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Cows graze on a green hillside in a photograph for the Farm Security Administration in 1939. Dairy farms were a mainstay of rural America.
photos.k: What does a cow eat all day?

photos.t: Black Troops at the Memorial Day Parade, Washington, D.C.
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Royden Dixon photographed Black soldiers marching in a Memorial Day parade in Washington, D.C., in 1939. Black Americans served in segregated units in the U.S. military.
photos.k: Why did the military separate soldiers?

photos.t: Christmas Trees and Wreaths in a Store Window
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Christmas trees and wreaths fill a store window in a 1939 photograph. Holiday displays drew shoppers even in the late Depression.
photos.k: How do shops decorate for the holidays?

photos.t: Preparing for Take-Off at Glider Pilot Training
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Alfred T. Palmer photographed Marines preparing for a glider take-off at the training program at Parris Island, South Carolina. Gliders have no engines and are towed into the sky by airplanes.
photos.k: How does a glider stay up with no engine?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Alfred T. Palmer photographed Marine Corps gliders in flight over Parris Island, South Carolina. The gliders float behind tow planes.
photos.k: What does it look like to see a plane towing a glider?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Alfred T. Palmer photographed a large electric phosphate smelting furnace used to make elemental phosphorus. The furnace glows as workers handle it.
photos.k: What is phosphorus used for?

photos.t: Girl Inspector at an Aircraft Plant
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Alfred T. Palmer photographed a woman inspector examining aircraft parts at a plant in Long Beach, California. During the war many women worked in factories.
photos.k: How would you check a part for flaws?

photos.t: Garden of the Pan American Union Building
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Collier photographed the garden of the Pan American Union building in Washington, D.C. The building, with a tropical patio, was home to the organization that later became the Organization of American States.
photos.k: Why would a garden have tropical plants?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Frances Benjamin Johnston photographed the Berry House in Selma, Alabama, for her survey of the Early Architecture of the South. Selma had many old buildings.
photos.k: What would you notice about an old house?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Frances Benjamin Johnston photographed the St. James Hotel in Selma, Alabama, in 1939. The three-story brick hotel stands beside the Alabama River.
photos.k: Why would a hotel be built beside a river?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Frances Benjamin Johnston photographed Riverdale Plantation near Selma, Alabama, in the late 1930s. She documented old southern houses for the Carnegie Survey of the Architecture of the South.
photos.k: Why would someone photograph old houses?

photos.t: Fashion Model Underwater with a Diver in a Dolphin Tank
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed a fashion model underwater with a diver in the dolphin tank at Marineland, Florida, in 1939. She tried odd places for fashion photographs.
photos.k: Would you pose underwater?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed a fashion model floating underwater in the dolphin tank at Marineland, Florida. Frissell took fashion photographs in outdoor and unusual spots.
photos.k: How would you pose in water?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Pie Town got its name from a woman who baked pies for travelers. Russell Lee photographed its homesteader families in color in 1940, and the pictures give a vivid look at a farming community. Here people gather outside a log church.
photos.k: What does the church building look like?

photos.why: Smoking stacks and giant furnaces fill the sky at a steel mill in Maryland. John Vachon photographed American towns and factories for the Farm Security Administration.
photos.k: What do you think steel was used for?

photos.why: John Vachon photographed the tall buildings of Chicago's Michigan Avenue from a street corner. Chicago invented the skyscraper, and this street shows why people loved the city.
photos.k: How many tall buildings can you count?

photos.why: Marion Post Wolcott photographed children in the American South on color film. At a time when most photographs were black-and-white, her color pictures show warm clothing and sunlight.
photos.k: What color do you notice first?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Four girls smile in a classroom in a small New Mexico town. Russell Lee photographed their one-room school and the children who came from farms for miles around.
photos.k: What would it be like to go to a one-room school?

photos.t: A Rainy Day in Providence, Rhode Island
photos.why: Britt Fuller photographed Providence, Rhode Island, in a downpour in December 1940. Rain on streets and roofs makes a moody scene.
photos.k: What does a rainy city sound like?

photos.why: This is a seated portrait of Agnes Sligh Turnbull, an American author of novels about small-town life, around 1940. She wrote The Rolling Years.
photos.k: What kind of stories would you tell about your town?

photos.t: Orson Welles with Virginia and Christopher
photos.why: Orson Welles, who directed Citizen Kane, poses with his wife Virginia and their daughter Christopher around 1940. He had become famous with his radio broadcast of The War of the Worlds in 1938.
photos.k: Why would a radio show scare listeners?

photos.why: This photograph shows the lounge inside the Twelfth Street YMCA in Washington, D.C., around 1940. The YMCA was an important gathering place for Black Washingtonians.
photos.k: Why would a community center matter?

photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed Yellowstone's geysers for a US government project that was supposed to produce murals for the Department of the Interior. The murals were never finished, but his photographs are now in the National Archives.
photos.k: What do you think the steam smells like?

photos.why: Taos Pueblo in New Mexico has multi-story adobe homes where people have lived for about a thousand years. Ansel Adams photographed it under a pale sky for a government project.
photos.k: Why might people build their homes in stacks like this?

photos.t: A Street Corner in Burlington, Vermont
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a street corner in Burlington, Vermont, in 1941 for the Farm Security Administration. A few cars and shops line the busy corner.
photos.k: What shops would you find on a corner?

photos.t: A Slate Quarry near Castleton, Vermont
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a slate quarry near Castleton, Vermont, in 1941. Slate is cut into roofing tiles and blackboards.
photos.k: What would you use slate for?

photos.why: Jack Delano photographed French-Canadian farmers in Vermont in 1941. Many families had moved from Quebec to work the dairy farms of the region.
photos.k: Why do families move to another country?

photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed a flock of sheep in the Owens Valley, California, in 1941. The sheep trail over the dry valley below the Sierra Nevada.
photos.k: What do shepherds do all day?

photos.why: Jack Delano photographed the main street of Enosburg Falls, Vermont, in 1941. The town was known for a patent medicine company.
photos.k: What do you see along the street?

photos.why: Ansel Adams photographed Walpi, a Hopi village on a high mesa in Arizona, in 1941. The pueblo has been lived in for hundreds of years.
photos.k: How would it be to live on top of a mesa?

photos.why: This is the cover of The Battle of Waterloo Road, a 1941 book about the London Blitz by the photographer Robert Capa. Capa photographed war around the world.
photos.k: Why would a war photographer take such risks?

photos.t: Road on the Outskirts of Brattleboro, Vermont
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a road on the edge of Brattleboro, Vermont, in 1941. Hills and a bend invite the eye.
photos.k: Where do you think the road leads?

photos.why: Britt Fuller photographed a snowy street corner in Brockton, Massachusetts, in January 1941. Brockton winters are cold.
photos.k: What do you wear on a winter day?

photos.why: This portrait shows Winston Churchill, the British prime minister during World War II, around 1941. His speeches inspired Britain.
photos.k: Why did people need inspiring speeches in the war?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: A woman operates a drilling machine in a factory making airplanes during World War II. Women like her took jobs that men had left to go to war, and posters called them Rosie the Riveter.
photos.k: What would you build if you worked in a factory?

photos.why: A tank kicks up a cloud of dust under a bright blue sky in this color photograph from 1942. Alfred Palmer photographed tanks being tested at an arsenal in Michigan, where factories that once built cars built weapons for World War II.
photos.k: What do you hear when a tank roars past?

photos.why: A street corner shop with a bright awning, ads and an old car outside, photographed in color in 1942. Most photos from this time are black-and-white, so color shows how lively ordinary streets were.
photos.k: What would you buy at a fruit store like this?

photos.t: The Tetons and the Snake River
photos.why: The Snake River curls through a valley below the jagged Teton Range in Wyoming. Ansel Adams's picture is one of the most famous landscapes ever made. It was even included on the Voyager spacecraft's Golden Record, sent out into the solar system.
photos.k: If aliens saw this picture, what would they think?

photos.why: Gordon Parks, then a young photographer, photographed Ella Watson, a cleaning woman, standing in front of an American flag with a mop and broom. He named it after a famous painting, and it was a quiet protest against racism in the nation's capital.
photos.k: What do you think Ella Watson would say about her life?

photos.t: 5000 Danish Seamen Sailing for the United Nations
photos.why: Louise Dahl-Wolfe photographed the Danish seamen who sailed with the Allies in 1942. Denmark had been occupied, but its sailors joined the war effort.
photos.k: Why would sailors leave an occupied country?

photos.why: Prime Minister William Lyon Mackenzie King of Canada, photographed in 1942. He led Canada through World War II.
photos.k: What does a prime minister do?

photos.t: Women Working in a Needlework Factory, Santurce
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed women working in a needlework factory in Santurce, Puerto Rico, in January 1942. Needlework was an important industry for women on the island.
photos.k: What would you embroider?

photos.t: Portrait of a Young Man, Southwest Washington, D.C.
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed a young Black man in Washington, D.C., in 1942. Parks was the first Black photographer on the Farm Security Administration staff.
photos.k: What would you ask the young man?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed A. Philip Randolph, the labor leader, in Washington, D.C., in 1942. Randolph led the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters and later organized the March on Washington.
photos.k: What does a labor leader do?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed a street in Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1942. The year can be told from the license plates of the cars.
photos.k: How can a license plate tell the year?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed a small grocery store along Route 74 in Mount Orab, Ohio, in 1942. Signs on the front advertise products of the day.
photos.k: What would you buy at a grocery in 1942?

photos.t: Eagle Fruit Store and Capital Hotel, Lincoln
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed the Eagle Fruit Store and the Capital Hotel in Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1942. The block has shop signs and cars lined up.
photos.k: What do the signs tell you?

photos.t: Cemetery at the Edge of Romney, West Virginia
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed a hillside cemetery at the edge of Romney, West Virginia, in 1942. Gravestones stand on a hill above the town.
photos.k: Why are cemeteries on hills?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed a country church near Junction City, Kansas, in 1942. The plain white church stands alone in a wide landscape.
photos.k: Why would a church stand alone in a field?

photos.t: Seed and Feed Store, Lincoln, Nebraska
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: John Vachon photographed a seed and feed store in Lincoln, Nebraska, in 1942. Farmers bought seed, grain and supplies there.
photos.k: What would a farmer buy at a feed store?

photos.t: Working on a Vengeance Dive Bomber
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: During World War II, millions of women took jobs in factories. Alfred Palmer photographed women at the Vultee plant in Tennessee as they worked on a dive bomber. His color pictures were meant to show Americans pulling together.
photos.k: What jobs do you think the women are doing?

photos.why: A young girl holds a box camera and takes a photograph in Washington, D.C. Esther Bubley photographed ordinary American life, including children and their hobbies.
photos.k: What would you photograph if you held a camera like this?

photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed the great jazz bandleader Duke Ellington at a table with friends in a lively club. Parks became the first Black photographer on the staff of Life magazine.
photos.k: What kind of music do you imagine they were listening to?

photos.t: Times Square on a Rainy Day
photos.why: The rain makes the pavement shine at Times Square in New York. John Vachon photographed the glittering signs and umbrellas during the war.
photos.k: What colors would the neon signs be?

photos.why: During World War II, the US government forced about 120,000 people of Japanese ancestry from their homes into camps like Manzanar in California. Ansel Adams photographed daily life there, including young people stretching in the morning.
photos.k: Why do you think it is important to remember what happened?

photos.why: President Franklin D. Roosevelt, Prime Minister Winston Churchill and Soviet leader Joseph Stalin met in Tehran, Iran, in 1943 to plan how to win the war. The photograph of the three sitting together became famous around the world.
photos.k: What do you think they are talking about?

photos.t: Duke Ellington at the Hurricane Ballroom
photos.why: A saxophone player performs under the lights at New York's Hurricane Ballroom. Duke Ellington's orchestra was one of the greatest in jazz.
photos.k: How would you play a saxophone?

photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a Chicago rail yard in color, with the Wrigley Building and other skyscrapers in the background. Trains moved the soldiers, food and goods that powered the war effort.
photos.k: What do the trains carry?

photos.why: A woman kneels to place flowers on a soldier's grave at Arlington National Cemetery on Memorial Day. White stones stretch into the distance, and a war was still going on. Esther Bubley photographed it for the Office of War Information.
photos.k: Who do you think she is remembering?

photos.t: Engineer Climbing into the Cab of His Engine, Cicero, Illinois
photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a locomotive engineer climbing into his engine in Cicero, Illinois, in 1943. Railroads were crucial for moving people and supplies during the war.
photos.k: What would you check before starting a locomotive?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed Frederick Marquis, the 1st Earl of Woolton, who was Britain's Minister of Food in World War II. He ran the rationing system.
photos.k: What is rationing?

photos.why: Jack Delano photographed a double-header Pennsylvania Railroad train, two locomotives pulling together, in Chicago in 1943. Big trains were needed for wartime freight.
photos.k: Why would a train have two engines?

photos.t: Enlisted Personnel Exercise on the Flight Deck of USS Lexington
photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed sailors exercising on the flight deck of the aircraft carrier USS Lexington in 1943. Steichen led a team of photographers for the U.S. Navy.
photos.k: How would you exercise on a ship?

photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed the chart room of the USS Lexington in 1943. Navigators plotted the ship's path on charts.
photos.k: How do you plan a path on the ocean?

photos.t: Rear Admiral John S. McCain Sr.
photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed Rear Admiral John S. McCain Sr. in 1943. McCain's son and grandson also became admirals and senators.
photos.k: Why would a family have many sailors?

photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed pilots of the USS Lexington celebrating in 1943 after air battles. Their faces show relief and joy.
photos.k: What would you do after a hard day's work?

photos.t: Inspection Aboard a U.S. Submarine, New London
photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed sailors lined up for inspection on a U.S. submarine at New London, Connecticut, in 1943. Submarine crews lived in tight quarters.
photos.k: What would it be like to live on a submarine?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed Princess Elizabeth in 1943, when she was a teenager. She became Queen Elizabeth II in 1952.
photos.k: How does a photographer capture a future queen?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed Alan Brooke, 1st Viscount Alanbrooke, the chief of Britain's Imperial General Staff, in the 1940s. Brooke guided British strategy in World War II.
photos.k: What does the portrait tell you about his job?

photos.t: F6F Going Down the Deck for Take-Off
photos.why: A U.S. Navy photographer made this picture of an F6F Hellcat fighter speeding down the flight deck of USS Lexington in 1943. Taking off from a ship was tricky.
photos.k: How does a plane take off on such a short runway?

photos.why: Jack Delano photographed the Atchison, Topeka and Santa Fe locomotive Number 5000, called Madam Queen, in 1943. The huge steam engine had a 2-10-4 wheel arrangement.
photos.k: What does a steam locomotive sound like?

photos.t: USS North Carolina Underway in the Gilbert Islands
photos.why: The battleship USS North Carolina steams through the Pacific near the Gilbert Islands in November 1943. The ship's big guns are pointed out to sea.
photos.k: Why are battleships so large?

photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed Rex Stewart, a trumpeter with Duke Ellington's orchestra, in 1943. Stewart was known for his half-valve trumpet sound.
photos.k: How would you make a trumpet sound different?

photos.t: Pilots Leaning Across an F6F on the USS Lexington
photos.why: Edward Steichen photographed pilots leaning across an F6F Hellcat on the USS Lexington in 1943. They are relaxed and ready.
photos.k: How would you relax before a flight?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed a bus driver in Daytona Beach, Florida, in 1943 for the Office of War Information. His portrait shows his uniform and pride.
photos.k: What do you think about the driver's job?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed Richard Wright in New York in 1943. Wright was the author of Native Son and Black Boy.
photos.k: Have you read a book by Richard Wright?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed the main street of Gloucester, Massachusetts, in 1943. The fishing town has narrow streets by the harbor.
photos.k: What jobs do people have in a fishing town?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed a Portuguese family in Gloucester, Massachusetts, in 1943. Many fishermen of Gloucester came from Portuguese families.
photos.k: How do families keep traditions in a new country?

photos.t: Women Workers Checking In, New Britain, Connecticut
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Gordon Parks photographed women workers checking in at the Fafnir Bearing Company in New Britain, Connecticut, in 1943. During the war women filled factory jobs.
photos.k: Why were so many women needed in factories?

photos.t: Children Playing in a Fountain, Dupont Circle
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed children playing in a fountain at Dupont Circle in Washington, D.C., in 1943. The splashing was a relief on a hot summer day.
photos.k: How do you cool off in summer?

photos.t: Waiting for a Bus at the Greyhound Terminal, Pittsburgh
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed passengers waiting at a Greyhound bus terminal in Pittsburgh in 1943. She traveled by Greyhound bus in 1943 to document wartime travel for the Office of War Information.
photos.k: What would you do while waiting for a bus?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed a starter calling out buses at the Greyhound terminal in Pittsburgh in 1943. The starter announced departures.
photos.k: How do airports announce flights today?

photos.t: A Greyhound Bus Driver Loading the Bus, Columbus
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed a Greyhound bus driver loading luggage in Columbus, Ohio, in 1943. Buses carried many wartime travelers.
photos.k: How would you pack a bus?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed travelers waiting for a bus at the Greyhound terminal in Cincinnati in 1943. Soldiers, workers and families crowd the benches.
photos.k: Who do you think is traveling?

photos.t: Passengers Boarding a Greyhound Bus, Cincinnati
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed passengers boarding a Greyhound bus at the Cincinnati terminal in 1943. Wartime travel was crowded, because gas was rationed and trains were full.
photos.k: Why was bus travel so crowded?

photos.t: Bus Trip from Knoxville to Washington
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Esther Bubley photographed passengers on a bus trip from Knoxville, Tennessee, to Washington, D.C., in 1943. Riders dozed, read and chatted over the long ride.
photos.k: What would you do on a long bus ride?

photos.t: U.S. Ships Under Attack Off Kwajalein
photos.why: Dark puffs of exploding shells fill the sky over a fleet of ships off Kwajalein in the Pacific. Edward Steichen, famous for art photographs, led the US Navy photography unit in World War II.
photos.k: What can a photograph show that a report can't?

photos.why: On June 6, 1944, D-Day, Allied soldiers waded ashore at Omaha Beach in Normandy, France, under heavy fire. Coast Guard photographer Robert Sargent took this picture of troops leaving their landing craft, and it became one of the best-known pictures of the invasion.
photos.k: What would you be thinking as you stepped off the boat?

photos.t: LCVP from a Landing Ship, Normandy
photos.why: A U.S. Navy photographer made this photograph of a landing craft carrying troops to the beaches of Normandy in 1944. LCVPs, or Higgins boats, carried soldiers from ships to shore on D-Day.
photos.k: What would it be like to ride toward a beach under fire?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed Henry L. Stimson, U.S. Secretary of War, in 1944. Stimson oversaw the American army in World War II.
photos.k: What does a Secretary of War do?

photos.why: Robert Capa photographed an American soldier in the water at Omaha Beach on D-Day, June 6, 1944. The soldier is crawling through the surf, with the beach under fire.
photos.k: What was the soldier probably thinking?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed Charles de Gaulle, leader of the Free French, in 1944. De Gaulle later became president of France.
photos.k: What does a leader's face show?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed General George C. Marshall, Army chief of staff in World War II. After the war Marshall created the Marshall Plan to rebuild Europe.
photos.k: Why would a general want to rebuild countries?

photos.why: Edward Weston photographed his cat Johnny sitting on a piece of driftwood in 1944. Weston, famous for sharp photographs of peppers and rocks, also took pictures of pets at his home in California.
photos.k: What shapes does the driftwood make?

photos.t: Raising the Flag on Iwo Jima
photos.why: On February 23, 1945, six US Marines raised the American flag on top of Mount Suribachi during the battle of Iwo Jima. Joe Rosenthal's photograph won the Pulitzer Prize and became the model for a famous memorial.
photos.k: How does the diagonal line of the flagpole make the picture feel?

photos.why: In May 1945, American troops liberated Ebensee, a Nazi concentration camp in Austria. The survivors in this photograph stare at the camera. Pictures like this showed the world what had happened and are kept as evidence so it is never forgotten.
photos.k: Why is it important to remember difficult history?

photos.why: On August 14, 1945, news of Japan's surrender set off wild celebrations in Times Square. In this picture by the US Navy photographer Victor Jorgensen, a sailor kisses a nurse, a joyful moment at the end of World War II.
photos.k: What do you see in the crowd that shows how people felt?

photos.why: The Tuskegee Airmen were the first African American military pilots in the US, trained in Alabama. They flew thousands of missions in World War II. Toni Frissell photographed one of them in Italy in 1945.
photos.k: Why was it important for the Tuskegee Airmen to prove themselves?

photos.why: Captain Edward Gleed, an Army Air Forces pilot with the Tuskegee Airmen, leans on his P-51 Mustang fighter in Italy in 1945. Toni Frissell photographed him in a sheepskin jacket, with his cap on.
photos.k: What do you think it was like to fly a fighter plane?

photos.cr: John L. Severance Fund
photos.why: Pim van Os made this abstract photograph just after World War II, using shapes and shadows instead of recognizable objects. He was a pioneer of abstract photography in the Netherlands.
photos.k: What shapes can you find? Do they look like anything?

photos.why: This photograph shows Princess Margriet of the Netherlands in 1945, the year she was born in Canada. Her family had fled the German occupation.
photos.k: Why was she born in Canada?

photos.why: This portrait shows Clement Attlee, who became the British prime minister in 1945 after Winston Churchill. He led the country in rebuilding after the war.
photos.k: What would you do first to rebuild after a war?

photos.t: New York Celebrating the Surrender of Japan
photos.why: Victor Jorgensen photographed New Yorkers celebrating the surrender of Japan on August 14, 1945. Confetti and paper fell from the windows of tall buildings, and the streets were full of cheering people.
photos.k: How would you celebrate the end of a long war?

photos.why: This photograph from 1946 shows a street in Safed, an old city in northern Israel known for its stone alleys. It comes from the PikiWiki archive of Israel.
photos.k: What do you notice about the stone alley?

photos.t: Fashion Model on the Edge of a Boat, Montego Bay
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed a fashion model on the edge of a boat as a man rows at Montego Bay, Jamaica, in 1946. She liked to shoot fashion outdoors in natural light.
photos.k: Why is outdoor light good for photographs?

photos.why: Yousuf Karsh photographed Brendan Bracken, a British politician and close friend of Winston Churchill, in 1947. Bracken was an early backer of the Financial Times.
photos.k: What does an adviser to a prime minister do?

photos.why: Orren Jack Turner photographed Albert Einstein in 1947. The scientist's wild hair and thoughtful look became a symbol of genius.
photos.k: What do you think he was thinking?

photos.why: Walter Kaudern photographed the town of Marovoay in Madagascar in 1947. The broad panorama shows rice fields and a river town.
photos.k: What would life by a river and rice fields be like?

photos.why: Carl Van Vechten photographed the French fashion designer Pierre Balmain with the American actress Ruth Ford in 1947. Balmain was one of the top designers in Paris.
photos.k: What does a fashion designer do?

photos.why: This photograph from Weeki Wachee Springs in Florida in 1947 shows a mermaid performer underwater. The Florida roadside attraction featured women who performed in the clear spring.
photos.k: How do mermaid performers breathe underwater?

photos.why: This 1947 photograph shows a Vietnamese family, Hoang Minh Dao and his wife and children. Family portraits record people in a time of change.
photos.k: What can a family photo tell you?

photos.t: Fashion Model in a Tennis Outfit, Seated on a Wall
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed a fashion model in a tennis outfit sitting on a wall in 1947. Frissell often posed models doing sports.
photos.k: How would you pose in sports clothes?

photos.t: Mayor D'Atilly Presents Press Photographers' Diplomas
photos.why: The Dutch National Archive photographed the mayor handing out diplomas to press photographers during the festive week of 1948 in Amsterdam. Press photographers came from around the world for the coronation of Queen Juliana.
photos.k: Why would a mayor give photographers diplomas?

photos.t: The Altalena on the Tel Aviv Coast
photos.why: Robert Capa photographed the ship Altalena on a beach in Tel Aviv in June 1948. The ship, carrying weapons for an Israeli militia, was shelled and burned during a conflict.
photos.k: Why would a ship be burned at sea?

photos.t: Frank Harriott, Karl Priebe, Edward Atkinson, Tom Kemp
photos.why: Carl Van Vechten photographed four men, Frank Harriott, Karl Priebe, Edward Atkinson and Tom Kemp, in 1948. Van Vechten photographed hundreds of artists and writers.
photos.k: Why would a photographer make portraits of so many creative people?

photos.why: Willem van de Poll photographed press photographers from home and abroad during festival week in 1948. They shared one crowded scene with many cameras.
photos.k: How many cameras can you count?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed a model called Mary Jane in 1948. Her pictures were published in fashion magazines like Harper's Bazaar.
photos.k: What does a fashion model do?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed the Tryall plantation house in Jamaica in 1948. The old house stands among palms and gardens.
photos.k: What would you do in a house in the tropics?

photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed a man sculling, or rowing with a single oar from the stern, in a boat off Jamaica in 1948. The water shines in the sun.
photos.k: How do you steer a boat with just one oar?

photos.t: Albert and Elsa Einstein in Caputh
photos.why: Lotte Jacobi photographed Albert and Elsa Einstein at their summer house in Caputh, near Berlin. They left Germany in 1933, and the house was later taken.
photos.k: Why would a family leave their home?

photos.why: This 1949 photograph from the PikiWiki archive shows a street in Peki'in, a village in northern Israel. Villagers have lived there for centuries.
photos.k: What do you see on the village street?

photos.t: Fashion Models Floating in a Swimming Pool
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Toni Frissell photographed fashion models floating in bathing suits in a swimming pool in 1949. The poses look like flowers on the water.
photos.k: How would you arrange people in a pool picture?

photos.t: Walking with Signs in a Civil Rights March
photos.cr: Library of Congress, Prints & Photographs Division
photos.why: Willie Brown and Doug Stewart walk with signs in a civil rights march in 1950. Activists marched for equal treatment long before the big marches of the 1960s.
photos.k: What would you put on a sign?
